title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Goals of This Section
In this section we will:

Lay out model for optimal taxation
Derive the Ramsey Rule for optimal commodity taxation
Discuss optimal user fees
Discuss optimal income taxation
Discuss political economy and time inconsistency
Discuss other criteria for tax design

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Introduction

As we have discussed, governments raise taxes mainly to raise revenue
But taxes involve costs

The direct cost of the revenue raised
Additional costs from distortions in behaviour (excess burden)

Given that revenue needs to be raised, how should taxes be designed to minimize costs?
Optimal taxation addresses this question

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Model

Question of optimal taxation is answered with a model
A representative citizen consumes two goods, \(X\) and \(Y\)

Prices of these goods are \(P_{X}\) and \(P_{Y}\)

Person can also work and earn wage \(w\)

Person has \(T\) hours available for work (\(h\)) or leisure (\(L\))
These are the only two uses of time, so \(T = h + L\)

Their budget constraint in this context is

\[ w(T - L) = P_{X}X + P_{Y}Y\]

Constraint says that income is split between spending on goods \(X\) and \(Y\)

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Model

If you rearrange the budget constraint, you can write it as

\[wT = P_{X}X + P_{Y}Y + wL\]

Shows that full income is split between spending on goods \(X\) and \(Y\) and spending on leisure

Full income is \(wT\) because if all time was worked, income would be \(wT\)
Price of leisure is \(w\) because each hour of leisure foregoes \(w\) in earnings

Suppose we tax goods \(X\), \(Y\), and \(L\) at rate \(t\)
Then the budget constraint becomes

\[ wT = (1 + t)P_{X}X + (1 + t)P_{Y}Y + (1 + t)wL\]

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Model

Rearranging gives

\[wT = (1+t)(P_{X}X + P_{Y}Y + wL)\]
\[ \frac{wT}{1 + t} = P_{X}X + P_{Y}Y + wL\]






Key Insight


A tax on all goods and leisure is equivalent to a reduction in full income by a factor of \(\frac{1}{1 + t}\)




We saw this in one of the practice questions

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Model






Why Taxing Everything Equally Is Non-Distortionary


If we could tax all goods and leisure at the same rate, we would not distort behaviour because relative prices are unchanged. The commodity taxes are equivalent to a lump-sum tax that reduces income.




But in practice, we cannot tax all goods and leisure at the same rate

We cannot tax leisure directly
Can only tax \(X\) and \(Y\) in this setup

Taxing some goods (\(X\) and \(Y\)) but not others (\(L\)) distorts relative prices and leads to excess burden

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Ramsey Rule

Question then becomes: If we cannot tax all goods at the same rate, how should we tax them?
One option is neutral taxation: taxing \(X\) and \(Y\) at the same rate

This is simple and easy to administer
But it still distorts behaviour and creates excess burden








The Ramsey Rule


Tax goods so that the percent reduction in quantity demanded is the same for all goods. Equivalently, tax goods so that the marginal excess burden of the last dollar of revenue raised is the same for all goods.




The next few slides establish this result

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Ramsey Rule

Consider again two goods, \(X\) and \(Y\), with prices \(P_{X}\) and \(P_{Y}\)
Pretend that goods are neither substitutes nor complements

Simplifies the analysis because changes in their prices do not affect each other’s demand
Results still hold for substitutes and complements, but analysis is more complex

Also pretend the supply curve is horizontal

Consumers face the entire economic incidence of the tax
Again simplifies the analysis because we do not have to consider supply side effects

Consider a unit tax \(u_{X}\) on good \(X\)

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Ramsey Rule





 










Consumer initially consumes \(X_{0}\) at price \(P_{0}\)
After tax \(u_{X}\) is imposed, price rises to \(P_{0} + u_{X}\)
Consumer reduces consumption to \(X_{1}\)
As we have learned this involves an excess burden

Equals area of yellow triangle
Represents the loss in consumer surplus beyond the tax revenue collected

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Ramsey Rule





 










Now imagine raising the tax further from \(u_{X}\) to \(u_{X} + 1\)
The additional excess burden created is the marginal excess burden

Equals area of purple trapezoid (triangle plus rectangle)

Part of that excess burden was tax revenue (purple rectangle)
Other part is additional loss in consumer surplus (purple triangle)

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Ramsey Rule

The marginal excess burden of the tax on good \(X\) is the purple area

Equals area of the purple triangle plus the purple rectangle

To compute that mathematically, set \(\Delta x = X_{1} - X_{2}\)
The total area is then

\[ (\frac{1}{2} \Delta x \times 1) + (\Delta x u_{X})  \]

As noted in the textbook, if we pretend that \(\frac{1}{2} \Delta x\) is very small, we can ignore it

So marginal excess burden is approximately \(\Delta x u_{X}\)

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Ramsey Rule

Going one step further, note that the slope of the demand curve is \[ \frac{u_{X}}{\Delta X} = \frac{1}{\Delta x} \]

\(\Delta X = X_{0} - X_{1}\), the initial change in quantity demanded from the initial tax
Both represent the rise over the run

Rearranging gives

\[ \Delta x u_{X} = \Delta X\]

The marginal excess burden of the tax on good \(X\) is approximately \(\Delta X\)

The change in quantity demanded from the initial tax

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Ramsey Rule

What about the change in revenue?
Initially revenue was larger green rectangle plus purple rectangle
After, it is larger green rectangle plus smaller green rectangle
The marginal tax revenue is therefore the smaller green rectangle minus the purple rectangle

\[ (X_{2} \times 1) - (\Delta x u_{X}) \]

We previously saw that \(\Delta x u_{X} = \Delta X\)
We also know that \(X_{2} = X_{1} - \Delta x\)
Subbing in gives us

\[ X_{1} - \Delta x - \Delta X  \]

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Ramsey Rule

If we pretend that \(\Delta x\) is very small, we can ignore it

So marginal tax revenue is approximately \(X_{1} - \Delta X\)

The marginal excess burden per dollar of additional revenue is

\[ \frac{\Delta X}{X_{1} - \Delta X} \]

If we repeat this exact exercise for good \(Y\), we find that the marginal excess burden per dollar of additional revenue is

\[ \frac{\Delta Y}{Y_{1} - \Delta Y} \]

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Ramsey Rule

If we set them equal

\[ \frac{\Delta X}{X_{1} - \Delta X} = \frac{\Delta Y}{Y_{1} - \Delta Y} \]

Which simplifies to the Ramsey Rule

\[ \frac{\Delta X}{X_{1}} = \frac{\Delta Y}{Y_{1}} \]

If you multiply both sides by \(100\) to express this as a percentage, it says percent change in quantity demanded of \(X\) equals percent change in quantity demanded of \(Y\)

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Ramsey Rule with Elasticities

Economists enjoy expressing things in terms of elasticities
The compensated price elasticity of demand is

\[ \eta_{X} = \frac{\Delta X}{\Delta P_{X}} \times \frac{P_{X}}{X} \]

Rearrange that to get

\[ \frac{\Delta X}{X} = \eta_{X} \times \frac{\Delta P_{X}}{P_{X}} \]

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Ramsey Rule with Elasticities

In this case, consider instead an ad valorem tax that makes the price rise to \(P_{X}(1 + t_{X})\)
The numerator of this fraction is then \(\Delta P_{X} = P_{X}(1+t_{X}) -  P_{X} = P_{X}t_{X}\)
Substituting into the equation on the previous slide gives

\[\frac{\Delta X}{X}  =  \eta_{X} \times t_{X}  \]

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Ramsey Rule with Elasticities

The Ramsey Rule then becomes

\[ \eta_{X} t_{X} = \eta_{Y} t_{Y} \]

Equivalently

\[ \frac{t_{X}}{t_{Y}} = \frac{\eta_{Y}}{\eta_{X}} \]

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Ramsey Rule with Elasticities






The Inverse Elasticity Rule


When goods are unrelated in consumption, the optimal tax rate on a good is inversely proportional to its compensated price elasticity of demand. If good \(Y\) has a high elasticity relative to good \(X\), then \(t_{X}\) should be higher than \(t_{Y}\).




Why?

Because a tax on a good with a high elasticity will cause a large reduction in quantity demanded
This creates a large excess burden
So to minimize excess burden, tax goods with high elasticities less

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Think About It
The inverse elasticity rule says we should tax goods with inelastic demand more heavily. Demand for food and medicine tends to be very inelastic, while demand for luxury goods like yachts and designer handbags tends to be more elastic. What does the Ramsey Rule imply about how we should tax these goods, and does that sit well with you? What might be missing from a purely efficiency-based approach to tax design?

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Corlett-Hague Rule

Recall that we could not tax leisure directly

And therefore could not apply an efficient (lump-sum equivalent) tax
This created the excess burden








The Corlett-Hague Rule


With two goods, tax the good that is complementary to leisure (used together with it) at the relatively higher rate. Examples: yachts, ski equipment, recreational vehicles.




This indirectly lowers demand for leisure and acts like a tax on leisure
Gets us a bit closer to the most efficient outcome

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Equity in Taxation

Ramsey rule implies taxing goods that are inelastic more heavily
Makes sense when those goods are socially undesirable (e.g., cigarettes, alcohol)
But what if those goods are necessities (e.g., food, clothing, housing, medicine)?
Problematic for a few reasons, but one is that it lacks vertical equity

Vertical equity: people with greater ability to pay should pay more in taxes

You can modify the Ramsey rule to account for vertical equity (Diamond, 1975)

A modified rule may tax necessities less heavily
Essentially allows for larger excess burden to achieve greater equity
How far to depart depends on how strongly society values equality, and how differently rich and poor consume



Diamond’s example: the poor spend a bigger share on bread, the rich on caviar. If social welfare weights the poor more heavily, it can pay to tax caviar at the higher rate even if bread is the more inelastic good. If society only cares about efficiency, stick with Ramsey. If rich and poor buy the two goods in the same proportions, different rates can’t redistribute anything, so there is no reason to depart.

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Think About It
Suppose a government must choose between two tax systems: one that minimizes excess burden (following the Ramsey Rule strictly) and one that is more equitable but generates a larger excess burden. How would you decide how much efficiency to sacrifice for equity? Is there a principle or framework that could guide this tradeoff?

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Summary

In the real world we cannot achieve the efficient outcome of a lump-sum tax to raise government revenue
Distortionary taxes change behaviour and create an excess burden
We can design the tax system to minimize the excess burden
The Ramsey Rule gives that optimal design
But tax efficiency is not the sole consideration

Equity is also important
The optimal rule can change to account for equity considerations

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Introduction

Governments often charge user fees for public services

User fee: a fee charged by the government for the use of a good or service
Examples: park entrance fees, toll roads, public transit fares, etc.

Like a tax, but not a tax
Determining the optimal user fee is similar to determining the optimal tax

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Government Production





 










Governments sometimes produce goods/services when there is a natural monopoly

Natural Monopoly: a market where a single firm can produce the entire output at lower cost than multiple firms
Happens with continuously decreasing average costs
Examples: water, electricity, public transit, etc.

Natural monopoly depicted to the left
Marginal cost fixed for ease of analysis

Could also draw it downward sloping as in the text

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Government Production





 










An unregulated monopolist would produce \(Q_{0}\) where MR = MC
Would charge price \(P_{0}\)
The monopoly earns excess profits equal to yellow area
Also associated with deadweight loss (excess burden) equal to red area
The monopolist does not produce the efficient (P=MC) level of Z

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Government Production





 










The government could take over and produce the good/service

Or regulate the private monopolist

There are different options for production
One is to produce the efficient level \(Q_{1}\) where \(P = MC\)
But price \(P_{1}\) is below average cost \(AC\)
The government would incur a loss equal to green area

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Government Production





 










Another option is average cost pricing
Produce \(Q_{3}\) where \(P = AC\)
Government incurs no excess profits or losses
Price \(P_{3}\) is above \(MC\), so there is still some deadweight loss (excess burden) equal to red area

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Government Production

A third option is to set P=MC and charge a lump sum tax to cover the loss

Hard to do in practice because generally cannot levy lump sum taxes
Non-users would pay for it, violating the benefits-received principle: those who use a public service should pay for it

A fourth option is a two-part tariff

Set P=MC and charge a fixed fee to cover the loss
Only users of the good pay the fee
Divide the loss by the number of users to get the fee per user
Drawbacks

Light users may quit rather than pay the fee, so use falls below the efficient level
Everyone pays the same fee, so it is regressive

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Government Production

Lastly, use the Ramsey Rule

If government produces multiple goods/services, set user fees for each
Optimally set them so that the percent reduction in quantity demanded is the same for all goods/services
We saw that this involves setting higher fees for goods/services with inelastic demand
The user fee effectively acts like a tax on the good/service

In practice, Canada uses average cost pricing in many cases for public and regulated enterprises

Inefficient, but simple and consistent with the benefits-received principle

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Think About It
Consider public transit in a city. Marginal cost pricing would set fares very low (since one extra rider costs almost nothing), but transit systems have large fixed costs. If you were advising a city government, which pricing strategy would you recommend – marginal cost pricing with a subsidy, average cost pricing, or a two-part tariff? What are the equity implications of each approach for low-income riders?

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Introduction

So far we have discussed optimal commodity taxes and user fees
Income taxes are another major source of government revenue
Income taxes are different because they tax a person’s ability to pay

One common view is that income measures ability to pay (we return to this under horizontal equity)
Income taxes therefore affect both labour supply and consumption

You can design an income tax optimally

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Old School Optimal Tax

A very old approach to optimal income taxation is Edgeworth’s Model







Edgeworth’s Model Assumptions



Maximize social welfare: the combination of individual utilities
Social welfare is utilitarian: the sum of individual utilities
Everyone has an identical utility function that depends only on income
Has diminishing marginal utility of income
Total amount of income in society is fixed





This model predicts that after-tax income is the same for everyone

Involves taxing rich and giving to poor until equality is reached
Incomes are levelled from the top down: a 100% marginal tax rate on the highest incomes

This is not a realistic model, but it is a starting point

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Newer Approach to Optimal Tax

Major problem with Edgeworth’s model is that it ignores behavioural responses

People will supply less labour if taxed heavily

Modern models take this into account

Taxes raise revenue that pays for redistribution
But also create excess burden by distorting labour supply
Optimal tax balances these two effects

The government chooses a tax schedule: the tax owed at each level of income

The schedule could take any shape, which makes the problem hard to solve
The simplest case is a straight line: a linear income tax
Not as limiting as it sounds: the optimal non-linear tax is close to linear (Mankiw, Weinzierl and Yagan, 2009)

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Newer Approach to Optimal Tax





 










A linear income tax schedule is depicted to the left
Revenue collected from a person with a given income is

\[ Revenue = -\alpha + t \times Income \]

The term \(\alpha\) is a fixed payment to everyone

If \(\alpha > 0\), it is a subsidy
If \(\alpha < 0\), it is a lump-sum tax

The term \(t\) is the marginal income tax

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Newer Approach to Optimal Tax





 










A constant marginal tax is a flat tax

Comes from a linear tax schedule

With the grant, it is still a progressive tax system

Share of income paid in tax rises with income

Canada and the US have marginal rates that rise with income

Optimal tax result: top rate should be lower than the bottom rate (Gruber and Saez, 2002)

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Newer Approach to Optimal Tax





 
















An example with different flat taxes is shown to the left
Graph plots total revenue
There are three curves

\(\alpha = 3000\), \(t = 0.25\)
\(\alpha = 5000\), \(t = 0.25\)
\(\alpha = 3000\), \(t = 0.5\)

\(\alpha\) changes the intercept
\(t\) changes the slope

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Newer Approach to Optimal Tax





 
















Now plot the proportion of income paid in tax
Here you can see the progressivity of the tax
With the same \(t\), the bigger grant, \(\alpha = 5000\), is the most progressive
Raising \(t\) with the same grant shifts the curve up without making it steeper
In the optimal tax problem, a higher \(t\) pays for a larger grant

The tax becomes more progressive, at the cost of more excess burden




The average tax rate is \(t - \alpha/\text{income}\). The grant term shrinks as income rises, which is what makes a flat tax progressive, and a bigger grant makes the average rate climb faster. Raising \(t\) adds the same amount at every income. In the optimal tax problem the two are tied together by the revenue requirement: a bigger grant has to be paid for with a higher \(t\), and a higher \(t\) means more excess burden. The book says simply that a higher \(t\) makes the system more progressive; that is the case where the extra revenue pays for a bigger grant. The slide holds the grant fixed to separate the two effects.

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Newer Approach to Optimal Tax

The specific optimal tax rates depend on the model assumptions

Labour supply elasticity: more elastic labour supply means a lower optimal \(t\)
Social welfare function
Ability to pay
Income distribution

Mankiw, Weinzierl and Yagan (2009): optimal \(t\) is around 48–50%

Optimal grant \(\alpha\) is just over 60% of average income per worker

Using a more egalitarian social welfare function, optimal tax is higher

Egalitarian social welfare function puts more weight on poorer individuals
Stern (1976), maximin criterion: optimal rate around 80%

Gruber and Saez (2002), four brackets: the top bracket gets a lower marginal rate than the lowest bracket

But average rates still rise with income, so the tax is still progressive



Why elasticity matters: the cost of redistributing is the excess burden it creates, and the more elastic labour supply is, the bigger that burden. Mankiw, Weinzierl and Yagan’s 48–50% is far below Edgeworth’s 100%, so even modest work responses matter a lot. Maximin puts all the weight on the worst-off person, and even then the rate stops short of 100%. Gruber and Saez: a lower top rate gets more work out of high earners, and the extra revenue lowers taxes at the bottom. The chapter summary states the stronger textbook result: the marginal rate on the very highest income should be zero, since taxing income above the top earner raises no revenue but still discourages that person’s work. Don’t oversell the precision here: the welfare function is a value judgement and the elasticities are uncertain.

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Introduction

Optimal tax theory provides purely theoretical guidance on how to design taxes
In practice, tax policy is determined by politics

Politicians care about getting elected
Voters care about their own taxes and benefits

So the optimal tax is not a realistic outcome
It is possible that in the real world, implementing the optimal tax is not even desirable (Holcombe, 2002)

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Time Inconsistency Problem

In 2012 the UK deputy prime minister proposed a one-time tax on the wealth of the rich (Frank, 2012)

It taxes wealth already built up, so it works like a lump-sum tax: no excess burden

But the government has an incentive to renege and do it again next year

The wealthy expect this and save less, so the tax distorts behaviour after all

Unless the promise is credible, the efficient policy can’t be carried out







Time Inconsistency Problem


A policy is time inconsistent when the government announces it but later has an incentive to abandon it. If people expect this, the announcement is not credible, and they act on what they expect the government to do rather than on what it says. An optimal tax plan can fail for this reason.




The government needs a way to commit, for example constitutional limits on going back on its word. As long as the incentive to renege is there, people will stay suspicious. The lesson: before recommending a policy from optimal tax theory, ask whether the government can credibly stick to it.

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Time Inconsistency Problem

Citizens are cynical

They think the government will implement the tax on \(Y\) but not lower it on \(X\)
View the government as trying to maximize revenue at their expense
In certain situations they might be right

If they are correct, taxing only \(X\) is more efficient than the alternative of taxing both







Time Inconsistency Problem


Optimal tax policy is not credible over time. The government cannot commit to future policies. To fully implement optimal tax, the government must credibly commit to future policies – this is difficult in practice, so optimal tax may not be achievable or even desirable.

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Think About It
Can you think of a real-world example where a government introduced a tax that was supposed to be temporary or offset by other changes, but ended up becoming permanent or expanding? What mechanisms could be put in place to help governments credibly commit to tax policy promises?

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Horizontal Equity






Horizontal Equity


People in “equal positions” should be treated equally. When it comes to taxation, equal positions might mean equal ability to pay, out of income, consumption, or wealth.




Horizontal equity is desirable because it is viewed as fair

People in equal positions should pay the same tax
If not, people may view the tax system as unfair and try to avoid taxes

Defining horizontal equity in terms of income or wage is problematic

Two people with the same wage who work different hours have different incomes but the same earning capacity
So they are arguably in equal positions, and income is a poor measure of position
Using the wage rate instead has problems: it reflects human capital investments, and hours are hard to observe and can be misreported

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Horizontal Equity

Could instead define horizontal equity in terms of utility (Feldstein, 1976)

Utility definition of horizontal equity: people with the same pre-tax utility should have the same after-tax utility, and taxes should not alter the utility ordering

Several problems with this approach

Utility is unobservable
If tastes differ, any income tax violates it: people who value goods bought with income are hit harder than people who value leisure

Some jobs pay partly in untaxed amenities (e.g. nice work environment, flexible work)

With identical tastes and free choice of job, pre-tax wages adjust until net returns are equal
So this is a horizontal inequity under the traditional definition, but not under the utility definition



Tastes: the book’s gourmets and sunbathers start equally well off. A proportional income tax hurts the gourmets more, because they need income to buy food, while the sunbathers mostly want leisure, which isn’t taxed. Amenities: if the job with the pool and the nice office came out ahead after tax, people would move into it, and the extra supply of workers would push its pre-tax wage down until the two jobs were equally attractive again.

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Administrative Costs

Taxes are costly to administer

Direct costs of about $1 to collect $100 of personal income and payroll tax (Vaillancourt, 1989)

Ignoring administration can backfire: cigarette smuggling in 1993–94

Combined federal and provincial taxes reached $2.75–$3 a pack, and smuggling from the US became rampant
Taxes were cut by up to 60% in Quebec and Ontario, and Ottawa stepped up border enforcement

Tax design must balance excess burden against administrative costs

E.g. a different rate on every good, as the Ramsey rule suggests, is cumbersome to run

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Compliance

Canada and other countries operate on a self-assessment system

Taxpayers are responsible for reporting their income and calculating their taxes
Government audits a small percentage of taxpayers to ensure compliance

Some people try to pay less tax

Tax avoidance: legally changing your behaviour to reduce your tax liability
Tax evasion: illegally not paying taxes you legally owe

It is not always easy to catch tax evasion

Government has to balance the costs of enforcement against the benefits
If enforcement is too costly, it may not be worth it

There is an economic theory that determines “optimal” tax evasion

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Compliance





 










Imagine that costs of evasion rise with the amount evaded

Penalty rises with amount evaded
There is some probability that you get caught
Could be psychic costs to cheating
Risk aversion might play a role

Benefit is constant

Gain is \(t\) per $1 evaded

As with many economic decisions, optimal evasion occurs where marginal benefit equals marginal cost
This person would evade \(R^{*}\)

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Compliance





 










If costs are too high, no evasion occurs

Probability of getting caught might be high
Penalty might be high
Large psychic costs or very risk averse

A higher audit probability or a higher penalty shifts marginal cost up, so evasion falls
Evidence: we don’t know whether bigger fines or more audits deter more

Audits raise later compliance for most groups, but the effect is small (Blumenthal, Christian and Slemrod, 2001)

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Compliance

Also the normative question about tax evasion: do we care about the welfare of evaders?
Some economies have large underground or informal economies

Developing countries often have significant employment in informal economies

Hiding legal work from the tax authorities is still tax evasion, so many informal workers are evaders
If their welfare counts, it might be desirable to have the underground/informal economy even if they pay no tax

They are often poor and would not pay much tax; some would be jobless under regular taxes and rules
They often provide goods/services that are beneficial to society
Trying to eliminate the informal economy might do more harm than good



Two more reasons from optimal tax theory if evaders’ welfare counts. If labour supply to the underground economy is more elastic, the inverse elasticity rule says it should be taxed lightly anyway. If it employs people who would be unemployed under regular taxes and rules like the minimum wage, an egalitarian society might want to leave it alone. If evaders’ welfare doesn’t count, the goal is just to stop cheating at the lowest cost: the penalty can always be raised high enough, but we don’t do that because we care about just punishment, not only the result.

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Summary

Taxes create excess burden by distorting behaviour
The Ramsey Rule gives the optimal way to tax goods to minimize excess burden
User fees can be optimized in a similar manner
Optimal income tax is progressive, but the specific rates depend on model assumptions
Politics and time inconsistency can prevent optimal tax from being implemented
Other criteria for tax design include horizontal equity, administrative costs, and compliance

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
References

Rosen, Harvey S., Lindsay M. Tedds, Trevor Tombe, Jean-François Wen, and Tracy Snoddon. Public Finance in Canada. 6th Canadian edition. McGraw-Hill Ryerson, 2023.
Gruber, Jonathan. Public Finance and Public Policy. 7th edition. Worth Publishers, 2022.
Studies cited by author and year on the slides are as reported in Rosen et al. (2023), Chapter 16.

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Goals of This Section
In this section we will:

Provide an overview of how corporate taxes work in Canada
Discuss the incidence and excess burden of corporate taxes
Understand how corporate taxes affect investment and financing decisions
Discuss the taxation of multinational corporations
Explore ideas for corporate tax reform

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Introduction

So far we have discussed individual taxation
Corporations also pay taxes, and are taxed separately
A corporation is a type of business organization that

Is a legal entity that is separate from its owners
Is owned by shareholders
Can enter into contracts, own assets, and incur liabilities

The structure limits liability for shareholders

Shareholders are not personally liable for the corporation’s debts or legal obligations beyond their investment in the company

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Introduction

Corporations are important in terms of economic activity
Also in terms of the taxes they pay
Given they pay tax, there are efficiency and equity considerations

We will explore these in this chapter

Corporate taxation is a complex and politically sensitive topic

We will only cover the basics here

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Why Tax Corporations?

In Canada, we have a personal income tax

The income of a corporation will eventually be distributed to individuals
So it could be taxed with the personal income tax

Why have a separate tax for corporations?







Reasons for a Separate Corporate Tax



Corporations receive special privileges: limited liability, perpetual life, easy transfer of ownership
These things are valuable, and so it is reasonable to tax corporations for them

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Why Tax Corporations?

It also withholds taxes from foreign companies that operate in Canada

Without a corporate tax, foreign companies could avoid paying Canadian taxes on their Canadian income
The corporate tax ensures that foreign companies contribute to the cost of public goods and services in Canada

It allows the government to capture economic rents

Some large corporations earn economic rents due to their market power or unique resources
Taxing these rents is a way to raise revenue from them

It creates fairness with personal taxes

Without a corporate tax, individuals could avoid paying personal income taxes by channeling their income through corporations
The corporate tax helps to prevent this type of tax avoidance

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Think About It
If corporate income is eventually distributed to individuals and taxed under the personal income tax, is the corporate tax just a form of prepayment? Could we achieve the same policy goals – capturing rents, taxing foreign firms, preventing avoidance – without a separate corporate tax? Why or why not?

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Tax Rates

Corporate tax rates are less complex than personal income tax rates
There are three main rates:

General corporate tax rate
Small business tax rate on the first $500,000 of active business income
Manufacturing and processing rate

Income is taxed at both the federal and provincial level

Just like personal income

title: EC313 - Taxation
text: Tax Rates

title: EC313 - Taxation
text: Tax Rates

title: EC313 - Taxation
text: Tax Rates

title: EC313 - Taxation
text: Tax Rates

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Tax Rates

These tax rates determine the statutory incidence of the corporate tax
We know that statutory incidence is not the same as economic incidence
Later we will explore who actually bears the burden of the corporate tax

As before, it is complicated
But generally speaking, the economic incidence falls on capital owners and workers

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Wage Payments

Corporations pay wages to workers
This is a cost of doing business
Wage payments to labour are excluded from the corporate tax base

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Depreciation

Business expenses are deductible from taxable income
But not all expenses are the same
Some get used up quickly (e.g., office supplies)
Others last a long time (e.g., machinery, buildings)
For tax purposes, they are treated differently

For long-lasting assets, depreciation (the part consumed in the year) is used to allocate the cost over time
The depreciation is deducted from taxable income each year

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Depreciation

How does this work in practice?
Suppose a firm buys a machine for $1000 that lasts 10 years
If using the straight line method (deductions spread evenly), each year it can deduct $100 from its taxable income as depreciation
This reduces the firm’s taxable income and thus its tax liability

If the corporate tax rate is 20%, the firm saves $20 in taxes each year due to the depreciation deduction

The present value of this stream of tax savings is

\[PV = \frac{20}{(1+r)} + \frac{20}{(1+r)^2} + ... + \frac{20}{(1+r)^{10}}\]

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Depreciation

The tax deductions effectively reduce the cost of the asset to the firm

\[\text{After-tax cost} = 1000 - PV\]

More generally, the present value of the tax savings is

\[PV = \frac{D(1)\times t \times q}{(1+r)} + \frac{D(2)\times t \times q}{(1+r)^2} + ... + \frac{D(T)\times t \times q}{(1+r)^{T}}\]

where

\(D(n)\) is the share of the initial asset cost that can be deducted in year \(n\)
\(t\) is the corporate tax rate
\(q\) is the initial cost of the asset

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Depreciation

If you factor out the initial cost \(q\), you get

\[PV = q \times \left(\frac{D(1) \times t}{(1+r)} + \frac{D(2)\times t}{(1+r)^2} + ... + \frac{D(T)\times t}{(1+r)^{T}}\right)\]

If we call the term in brackets \(\psi\), then the tax savings is \(q \times \psi\)
The after-tax cost of the asset is then

\[\text{After-tax cost} = (1-\psi)q\]

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Depreciation

From that equation, the tax savings are higher if

The total depreciation schedule is shorter (smaller \(T\))
The total depreciation schedule is faster (\(D(n)\) bigger in earlier years)

This means that accelerated depreciation is more valuable for tax purposes
The most valuable is full expensing, where the entire cost can be deducted in the year of purchase
In Canada, certain investments are eligible for accelerated depreciation

Explained in detail here: https://www.canada.ca/en/revenue-agency/services/tax/businesses/topics/sole-proprietorships-partnerships/report-business-income-expenses/claiming-capital-cost-allowance/accelerated-investment-incentive.html

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Depreciation

An alternative to the straight line method is the declining balance method

Declining balance is more common in Canada

Under declining balance, a fixed percentage of the remaining undepreciated value is deducted each year
For example, if the declining balance rate is 20%, in the first year the firm deducts 20% of the initial cost, in the second year it deducts 20% of the remaining value after the first year’s deduction, and so on
This results in larger deductions in the earlier years and smaller deductions in later years

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Investment Tax Credits

In addition to depreciation deductions, firms may also be eligible for investment tax credits (ITCs)
Recall: deductions reduce taxable income, while credits reduce tax liability directly
ITCs are typically a percentage of the purchase price of investments
Reduce the tax liability in the year the investment is made
Example: a 10% ITC on a $1000 machine would reduce the firm’s tax liability by $100 in the year of purchase
Canada has used ITCs to encourage investment in certain sectors or regions

Manufacturing and processing, clean energy
Atlantic region

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Interest

Corporations can deduct interest payments on debt from their taxable income
Suppose the firm borrowed $1000 for 10 years at 10% interest

Each year, the firm pays $100 in interest

The firm can deduct this $100 from its taxable income each year

If the corporate tax rate is 20%, saves $20 in taxes each year

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Interest

The present value of this stream of tax savings from interest deductions is

\[PV = \frac{20}{(1+r)} + \frac{20}{(1+r)^2} + ... + \frac{20}{(1+r)^{10}}\]

In general, the present value of the tax savings from interest deductions is

\[PV = \frac{i \times q \times t}{(1+r)} + \frac{i \times q \times t}{(1+r)^2} + ... + \frac{i \times q \times t}{(1+r)^{T}}\]

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Interest

Factoring out the initial loan value \(q\), you get

\[PV = q \times \left(\frac{i \times t}{(1+r)} + \frac{i \times t}{(1+r)^2} + ... + \frac{i \times t}{(1+r)^{T}}\right)\]

If we call the term in brackets \(\lambda\), then the tax savings is \(q \times \lambda\)
The after-tax cost of the loan is then

\[\text{After-tax cost} = (1-\lambda)q\]

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Dividends

Dividends are a main way to extract profits from a corporation

They are payments made to shareholders from the corporation’s earnings

Dividends are taxed as personal income to the shareholders
They are not deductible from the corporation’s taxable income
Raises the question of double taxation

Corporation pays tax on its earnings
Shareholders pay tax on dividends received

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Dividends

To mitigate double taxation, Canada has a dividend gross-up and tax credit system
When shareholders receive dividends, they must “gross up” the dividend amount by a certain percentage to reflect the pre-tax income of the corporation
They then pay personal income tax on this grossed-up amount
To offset this, shareholders receive a dividend tax credit that reduces their personal tax liability
In the end, the total tax paid on corporate earnings distributed as dividends is intended to be roughly equivalent to the tax that would have been paid if the income were earned directly by the shareholders

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Dividend Tax Credit System

Imagine a corporation earns $125 in pre-tax profits
It pays a corporate tax of 20%, leaving $100 in after-tax profits
Distributing this $100 as a dividend to a shareholder
The shareholder grosses up the dividend by 25% (the gross-up rate for eligible dividends), resulting in a grossed-up amount of $125
The shareholder pays personal income tax on this $125
If the rate is 40%, the tax owed is $50

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Dividend Tax Credit System

The shareholder then receives a dividend tax credit to offset some of this tax
If the tax credit is 20% of the grossed-up amount, the credit is $25
The shareholder’s net tax liability on the dividend is then

Tax owed: $50
Minus tax credit: $25
Net tax liability: $25

Total tax paid on the original $125 of corporate profits is

Corporate tax: $25
Shareholder tax: $25
Total tax: $50

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Dividend Tax Credit System

Notice that this is the same as if the shareholder had earned the $125 directly and paid 40% personal income tax

It instead comes partly from the corporation and partly from the shareholder

This system helps to integrate corporate and personal taxation, reducing the double taxation of dividends




Currently in Canada for regular businesses

The federal gross-up rate for eligible dividends is 38%
The federal dividend tax credit rate is 15.02% of the grossed-up amount




For small businesses, the rates are different

The federal gross-up rate is 15%
The federal dividend tax credit rate is 9.03% of the grossed-up amount




There are also provincial variations

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Think About It
The dividend gross-up and tax credit system is designed to make the total tax on corporate earnings roughly equal to what individuals would pay if they earned the income directly. But does this integration work equally well for shareholders in different tax brackets? Who benefits most from any imperfections in the system?

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Retained Earnings

Corporations can retain earnings instead of distributing them as dividends
Retained earnings are reinvested in the business or held as cash reserves
Should a firm retain earnings or pay them out as dividends?



If given out as dividends

Shareholders pay personal income tax on the dividends received
Recall that because of the gross-up and tax credit system, this is roughly equivalent to personal income tax


If retained

No personal income tax
But value of shares increase
Shareholders pay capital gains, but only when they sell the shares
Inclusion rate is 50%

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Retained Earnings

Preferential treatment of capital gains creates an incentive to retain earnings

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Tax Expenditures






Definition


Tax expenditures are indirect ways the government spends money through the tax system – through deductions, credits, exemptions, and preferential rates.




Governments use both the personal and corporate tax systems for tax expenditures
Examples in the corporate tax system include

Charitable donation deduction
Film tax credit
Investment tax credit
Lower small business tax rates

All ways in which government targets assistance to particular activities or groups

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Effective Tax Rates

The statutory corporate tax rate is not the same as the effective tax rate
The effective tax rate takes into account deductions, credits, inflation, and other provisions that affect the actual tax paid
The combined federal + provincial statutory rate averages around 28%
The average effective tax rates vary from 7%-23%

Higher for larger firms and retail operations
Lowest for firms in forestry and manufacturing

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Effective Tax Rates

Inflation is one factor that can change the effective tax rate
Three main ways inflation affects corporate taxes

Undervalues deductions for goods in inventory, leads to higher taxable income
Depreciation is based on historical cost, not replacement cost, leading to higher taxable income
Interest deductions lead to lower taxable income

Deduction based on nominal interest, which includes an inflation component
Inflation component is not a real cost, so deduction is overstated

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Effective Tax Rates

Overall, inflation tends to increase the effective corporate tax rate
Studies show that adjusting for inflation can reduce corporate income tax substantially

Old studies showed that they would be about 40% lower
Strongest effects in capital-intensive industries like forestry
For some companies tax on real profits was greater than 100%

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Introduction

Two key concepts we have come back to throughout the course are

Incidence: who ultimately bears the burden of a tax
Excess burden: the efficiency cost of a tax beyond the revenue raised

We discussed in the context of consumption and personal income taxes
Corporate tax can also create these issues

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Tax Incidence

Suppose the government levies a corporate tax

The statutory incidence is on the corporation

Who bears the economic incidence?
If the corporation produces goods/services, it may shift some to consumers

Higher prices
Depends on price elasticity of demand

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Tax Incidence

Suppose the corporations bear some of the economic burden
In a general equilibrium setting, they can shift to other factors of production

Labour
Capital

If corporations employ a large share of workers

Supply may not be very elastic
Workers could bear some burden

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Tax Incidence

Corporate capital owners may also bear some burden

In the short run, capital may not be very mobile

Capital would bear a burden initially

In the longer run, it could move elsewhere

Increases elasticity
Burden on capital owners would be lower


If capital is more mobile than labour in the longer run, then workers would bear more of the burden

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Tax Incidence

The corporate tax can also affect investment decisions

The tax lowers the after-tax return
Investors would move to the non-corporate sector seeking higher returns
Increases supply of capital in non-corporate sector
Leads to lower returns there too

Investors in the non-corporate sector would therefore also bear some burden

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Excess Burden






Distortions from Corporate Taxes


Corporate taxes create a distortion in investment decisions:

Investors may shift away from corporate investments and toward other investments
Firms may choose to not incorporate despite the benefits
Creates a substitution effect
Shifts the allocation of capital in the economy away from the efficient level





The distortion leads to an excess burden

The loss in economic efficiency beyond the tax revenue raised

Estimates suggest that for each dollar of corporate tax revenue raised, there is an additional 50 cents of excess burden

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Think About It
If the corporate tax creates roughly 50 cents of excess burden for every dollar of revenue raised, is it still worth having? What would happen to the distribution of the tax burden if we abolished it and tried to raise the same revenue through the personal income tax instead?

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Introduction

As we have learned throughout the course, taxes alter behaviour
For corporate taxes we might expect three changes

The amount of investment in physical assets (equipment)
The types of investment in physical assets
How these investments are financed

We will cover each in turn

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Total Physical Investment

Consider a firm investing in a new machine
The cost of the machine in a particular year is

Depreciation: the direct cost of owning the machine that year
Opportunity cost: the return that could be earned if the money were invested elsewhere

Can express both as a percentage of each dollar invested

Depreciation might be 2%
Opportunity cost might be 10%

In example, only invest in new machine if return > 12%

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Total Physical Investment






User Cost of Capital


The cost of ownership of an asset is called the user cost of capital – the sum of the direct and opportunity costs. It equals the minimum earnings required for each one dollar investment.




In general you can express the user cost of capital as

\[C = r + d \]

Where

\(C\) is the earnings from the investment
\(r\) is the opportunity cost of capital (interest rate)
\(d\) is the depreciation rate of the asset

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Total Physical Investment

Corporate taxes add to these costs
Suppose the tax rate is \(t\)
Now the after-tax earnings must be as large as the costs
After-tax earnings are \((1-t)C\), which means

\[C(1-t) = r + d \]

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Total Physical Investment

Rearranging gives

\[C = \frac{r + d}{1-t} \]

The pre-tax user cost of capital is divided by (1 - t)
This grosses up the required earnings to cover the tax paid

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Total Physical Investment

Example

Suppose there are no taxes and \(r = 10\%\) and \(d = 2\%\)
The earnings required per dollar invested is \(C = 0.10 + 0.02 = 0.12\) or 12%
Now suppose there is a corporate tax of 45% (\(t = 0.45\))
The new required earnings is \(C = \frac{0.10 + 0.02}{1-0.45} = \frac{0.12}{0.55} = 0.2182\) or 21.82%

Need to earn more to cover the tax paid

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Total Physical Investment

Things get slightly more complicated when you consider deductions
Suppose the firm can deduct the whole expense of the asset
The after-tax user cost of capital is then

\[C = \frac{(r + d) - (r+d)t}{1 - t} = \frac{ (r+d)(1 - t)}{1 - t} = r+d\]

In this case, the corporate tax has no effect on the user cost of capital

Since no tax is paid on the investment

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Total Physical Investment

In reality, firms cannot deduct the full cost of an asset in the year of purchase

As we saw earlier, depreciation deductions spread the cost over time

In this case, the deductibility mitigates the cost, but not entirely
Suppose the deduction is equal to \(\psi\) of the cost

\[C = \frac{(r + d) - (r+d)\psi}{1 - t} = \frac{ (r+d)(1 - \psi)}{1 - t} \]

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Total Physical Investment

There may also be investment tax credits (ITCs) that further mitigate the cost
Suppose the ITC is equal to \(k\) of the cost
Then the user cost of capital is

\[C = \frac{(r + d) - (r+d)(\psi + k)}{1 - t} = \frac{ (r+d)(1 - \psi - k)}{1 - t} \]

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Total Physical Investment

Finally, a firm might finance the investment with debt
Interest payments are deductible from taxable income
Suppose the interest rate is \(\lambda\)
The user cost of capital is then

\[C = \frac{(r + d) - (r+d)(\psi + k + \lambda) }{1 - t} = \frac{ (r+d)(1 - \psi - k - \lambda )}{1 - t} \]

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Total Physical Investment






Key Takeaways on User Cost of Capital



Corporate taxes generally increase the user cost of capital
This reduces the incentive to invest in physical assets
Deductions, credits, and interest deductions can mitigate this effect
The overall impact depends on the specifics of the tax system and firm behaviour





Evidence supports the idea that tax incentives can affect investment

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Types of Investment

Tax incentives are not necessarily applied equally to all investments

In Canada manufacturers can use full expensing
Also full expensing for clean energy investments
Other eligible property allowed accelerated depreciation

This creates incentives to invest in certain types of assets over others
Table on next slide shows Marginal Effective Tax Rates for various types of investments in Canada

title: EC313 - Taxation
text: Types of Investment

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Financing Investments

Firms need to decide to pay dividends or retain earnings
Also how to finance an investment

Debt (loans, bonds)
Equity (issuing stock)

The tax system can affect these

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Financing Investments

We covered earlier that preferential tax treatment of capital gains creates an incentive to retain earnings

If $1 of earnings increases share value by $1
Gains on shares only taxed when sold
And only taxed on half the gains

So the tax system creates an incentive to retain earnings rather than pay dividends
Firms do retain substantial earnings, but also pay some dividends
Why would they do that when there is a tax incentive to retain?

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Financing Investments

One reason is signalling

Paying dividends can signal to investors that the firm is doing well
Investors may view dividend-paying firms as more stable and reliable
This can increase demand for the firm’s stock, raising its price

Second reason is differences in marginal tax rates

Some shareholders may have lower marginal tax rates
So dividends could offer a lower tax burden for them

Investors tend to flock to firms that offer the best financial policies

Called clientele effects

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Financing Investments

The tax system can also affect how firms finance investments
Interest payments on debt are deductible from taxable income
Dividends paid to shareholders are not deductible
This creates an incentive to finance investments with debt rather than equity

Raising a dollar through debt is cheaper than raising a dollar through equity

There are additional costs to debt financing (e.g., bankruptcy risk) that increase the non-monetary cost

So we would not expect to see everyone using only debt financing

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Discussion
The tax system encourages firms to finance with debt over equity, since interest is deductible but dividends are not. During the 2008 financial crisis, high levels of corporate debt amplified the downturn. Should the government remove the tax preference for debt to reduce financial fragility, even if it raises the cost of investment?

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Introduction

Canadian firms operate in most foreign countries
How does the corporate tax system handle income earned abroad?
We cover that in this section

Note that we do not cover the taxation of foreign firms operating in Canada

First cover the rules and then tax policy

title: EC313 - Taxation
section: Rules for Taxation of Foreign Income
text:
Rules for Taxation of Foreign Income

General principle is to be neutral with respect to where income is earned

Wants firms to face similar taxes here and abroad

But also wants to ensure Canadian government collects tax revenue

Avoid tax avoidance which erodes the tax base

Rules differentiate between active and passive income

Active income: business income from operations
Passive income: investment income (dividends, interest, royalties)

title: EC313 - Taxation
section: Rules for Taxation of Foreign Income
text:
Rules for Taxation of Foreign Income


Passive income

Included in taxable income when it is earned
Taxed at the Canadian corporate tax rate
Foreign tax credits available for taxes paid abroad


Active income

Of incorporated subsidiaries: taxed only in the source country

These are separate legal entities from the main business

Of branches: taxed in Canada when earned

Branches are not separate legal entities

title: EC313 - Taxation
section: Rules for Taxation of Foreign Income
text:
Rules for Taxation of Foreign Income

Corporate taxation of a firm operating in multiple countries can be problematic
Generally, Canadian firms use the arm’s length principle

Profits are each entity’s own sales minus costs

Can lead to transfer pricing issues

Firms may manipulate prices of goods/services traded between entities to shift profits to low-tax jurisdictions
Example: IP owned in low-tax country, charged high royalties to subsidiaries in high-tax countries

Royalties are tax deductible
Income is earned in low-tax country

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Tax Policy

We discuss two policy goals of the Canadian government

Maximize world income
Maximize national income

First imagine the goal is to maximize world income
Firms maximize global incomes when pre-tax returns are the same across countries

Want capital to move where it is most productive
This only happens when pre-tax returns are equalized
There are no distortions from taxes

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Tax Policy

Equal pre-tax returns happen when

\[ r_f = r_c \]

When taxes exist, firms distort their decisions and equalize after-tax returns

\[(1 - t_f)r_f = (1 - t_c)r_c\]

If goal is equal pre-tax returns, then need to set

\[ t_c = t_f \]

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Tax Policy

Means Canadian and foreign taxation needs to be equal

So no distortions are created

Canadian firms allow a tax credit up to the Canadian tax on foreign income

Cannot allow more than that or foreign firms could increase taxes to raise revenue without any consequence

The government may instead try to maximize national income

Focus on income that accrues to Canadian residents
Equals before tax income earned in Canada plus after-tax income earned abroad

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Tax Policy

In this instance, policy should be to equalize

\[ r_f (1 - t_f) = r_c \]

Means pre-tax Canadian returns equal after-tax foreign returns

Prioritizes income earned in Canada
Foreign income pre-tax needs to have higher return than Canadian

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Tax Policy

If Canada wants to maximize national income, then should set

\[ r_f (1 - t_f) (1-t_c)= r_c (1-t_c) \]

Sets the same tax rate on after-tax foreign income as on pre-tax Canadian income

Can do this by allowing foreign tax deduction

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Introduction

The current corporate tax system in Canada is complex
The treatment of dividends is in particular complicated

Taxed at both corporate and personal levels
Complex system of gross-ups and tax credits to mitigate double taxation

There have been calls for reforming the corporate tax system

Simplify the system
Improve efficiency and equity

We discuss a few of the current ideas

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Partnership Method






Partnership Method


The partnership method taxes income only once at the personal level – removes corporate taxation altogether and taxes shareholders on their share of corporate income at personal income rates.




Some benefits include

Less excess burden by removing corporate tax distortions

Eliminate misallocation of capital between corporate and non-corporate
Lower tax on capital overall
Less incentive for retained earnings
Less incentive for debt financing

More saving due to lower capital taxes

Increases investment and economic growth

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Partnership Method

Some potential issues

Administratively complex

Tracking income for many shareholders
How to treat short term shareholders

Problems with distribution of income

People with high personal tax rates benefit less
Benefit people with more income from capital more

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Other Methods








Dividend Exclusion



Make dividends non-taxable at personal level
Only taxed at corporate level











Dividend Deduction



Allow corporations to deduct dividends paid from taxable income
Only taxed at personal level











Dual Income Tax



Capital income taxed at lower rate to encourage investment
Labour income taxed at higher rate for progressivity

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Summary

Corporations are taxed separately from individuals
Depreciation, interest, and dividends have special tax treatments
Corporate taxes create incidence and excess burden issues
Taxes affect investment decisions and financing choices

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
References

Rosen, Harvey S., and Lindsay M. Tedds, and Trevor Tombe, and Jean-Francois Wen, and Tracy Snoddon. Public Finance in Canada. 6th Canadian edition. McGraw-Hill Ryerson, 2023.
Gruber, Jonathan. Public Finance and Public Policy. 7th edition. Worth Publishers, 2022.
Bazel, Philip. Marginal Effective Tax Rates for Working Families in Canada. Fraser Institute, 2024.
Hansen, Jeff, and Devan Mescall, and Graham Purse. “Policy Forum: The Effects of Indexation and Inflation on Tax System Design.” Canadian Tax Journal 71, no. 2 (2023): 398-404.

title: Assignment 1
text:
Description
On April 1, 2025, the federal carbon charge on fuel was set to zero, and British Columbia ended its own carbon tax on the same day. Quebec, which prices carbon through cap-and-trade instead, was unaffected. In this assignment you will use Statistics Canada data on gasoline prices to measure how much of the tax cut reached drivers at the pump, and use that measurement to work out who bore the carbon tax.
The assignment is designed to give you practice analysing data in R and writing up your results in Quarto, and to show how economists use a change in policy to measure the incidence of a tax.
Due: Friday, October 9, 2026 at 9:00pm.






Download both files into the same folder



 ec313assign1.qmd — the assignment questions, as a Quarto document you write your answers into
 ec313assign1.csv — the data

title: Assignment 1
text:
Instructions
The questions are in the Quarto document above. Open it in RStudio and press Render before you change anything: it should produce a PDF. If it does not, fix that first, using the Introduction to R and Quarto page.
Then work through the questions, writing your R code in the chunks provided and your answers in the text below each question. The hints under each question point to sections of the Introduction to R and Quarto page, which has a worked example of each step. Wherever a written answer is needed, the question has a Comment on the results prompt, just above the answer space, that says what to cover. Tables must be made with modelsummary(), datasummary() or datasummary_df(), and graphs must have readable axis labels. Do not copy and paste, or screenshot, console output.






Some of your answers are marked by computer



Several questions ask you to store a result under a particular name, such as q2 or pt_naive. Those objects are checked automatically, so:

use exactly the names given in the question;
do not change the code in the setup and load-data chunks;
do not round the numbers you store (round only when displaying them).

The last chunk in the document tells you whether any of the required objects are missing.

title: Assignment 1
text:
The data
The data come from Statistics Canada’s monthly survey of retail gasoline prices, Table 18-10-0001-01. They are the average price of regular unleaded gasoline at self-service stations in 15 cities, for each month from October 2024 to September 2025: six months before the carbon tax was removed and six months after, 180 rows in all.







Variable
Description




city
City


province
Province


date
The month, stored as a date (the first day of the month)


month
The month, as text, such as “2025-03” for March 2025


gas
Average price of regular gasoline, in cents per litre, including all taxes


salestax
The GST or HST rate charged on gasoline in the province (plus the QST in Quebec), as a proportion: 0.13 means 13%



Three cities in the Statistics Canada table are left out on purpose:

Winnipeg, because Manitoba’s gas tax holiday ended on January 1, 2025, adding 12.5 cents a litre of provincial tax in the middle of the period, for reasons that have nothing to do with the carbon tax.
Whitehorse and Yellowknife, because prices in the territories come from few stations and often do not change for months at a time.

One city that is kept has a second change to account for: Halifax, where the HST also fell from 15% to 14% on April 1, 2025. That lowered the price there by about one more cent.
Source: Statistics Canada, Table 18-10-0001-01, Monthly average retail prices for gasoline and fuel oil, by geography, October 2024 to September 2025. Reproduced and distributed on an “as is” basis with the permission of Statistics Canada.
