Gruber, Jonathan. Public Finance and Public Policy. 7th edition. Worth Publishers, 2022.
Finances of the Nation. https://financesofthenation.ca/
Department of Finance Canada. Spring Economic Update 2026. https://budget.canada.ca/update-miseajour/2026/

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Goals of This Section
In this section we will:

Examine the effect of income taxation on labour supply
Analyze how labour supply is related to tax revenues with the Laffer Curve
Look at how taxation affects saving behaviour
Discuss the preferential tax treatment of primary residences in Canada
Examine taxation and portfolio allocation

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Introduction

In this section we introduce a model we use throughout the course
The model helps us understand how individuals make decisions about work
Individuals choose between two goods

Income
Leisure

Choices are constrained by time and wage rate
There are a few wrinkles that make this market unique

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Preferences

Individuals have preferences over Income (I) and leisure (L)

People like having income to consume goods/services
Also like having non-work time

Includes fun activities but also non-work tasks like chores, education, etc.


The tradeoffs people are willing to make between I and L are represented by indifference curves

At every point along the curve the individual is equally happy
Curves further from the origin represent higher levels of utility

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Preferences





 










On the left is a single indifference curve
Any point represents equal utility (\(U_{0}\))







Marginal Rate of Substitution (MRS)


The rate at which a person is willing to trade income for leisure while remaining equally happy. The MRS is the slope of the indifference curve at a point.




Individuals have diminishing MRS

Willing to give up less income for additional leisure the more leisure they already have
Slope gets shallower with more leisure

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Preferences

Indifference curves do not have to be smooth curves like the one shown
Could be straight lines

Means the tradeoff between income and leisure is constant
Willingness to trade away leisure for income does not depend on leisure

Could be “L” shaped

Income and leisure must be consumed in fixed proportions

Mostly we will deal with smooth preferences

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Preferences





 










Utility increases with curves further from the origin

\(U_{2} > U_{1} > U_{0}\)

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Constraints

Individuals do not choose income and leisure bundles on preference alone
They are constrained by

The wage rate
Total number of hours available

Budget constraint is also called

Potential income constraint
Full income constraint

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Constraints





 










Graph shows a linear budget constraint
There are \(T\) total hours to allocate to work or leisure
Each hour worked gets wage of \(w\)
Person working \(T\) hours (no leisure) earns \(wT\) income

Called full income

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Constraints

Mathematically, the budget constraint is

\[I = w(T - L)\]

Income is equal to income from working \((w(T - L))\)
The slope of the budget constraint is \(-w\)

The opportunity cost of leisure is the wage rate
Each hour of leisure means one less hour worked, which means \(w\) less income

Someone who works zero hours has \(T\) leisure hours and no income
Someone who works \(T\) hours has zero leisure hours and \(wT\) income

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Constraints





 










Slope is the negative of the wage rate \(w\)
A lower wage means shallower slope

If \(w_{1} < w_{0}\), the budget line swivels down
They intersect at leisure = \(T\) because there are no work hours

Lower wage also means full income is lower

Working all hours leads to less total labour earnings

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Consumer Optimum

Work hours are chosen using the combination of preferences and constraints
The consumer optimum is the point that maximizes utility subject to the budget constraint
The optimum occurs where the budget constraint is tangent to an indifference curve
There are two possibilities for the optimum

Non-participation: optimum occurs at the end of the budget constraint (full leisure)
Participation: optimum occurs at an interior point (some leisure, some work)

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Consumer Optimum





 










Graph shows an optimum with participation
Optimum is where indifference curve is tangent to budget constraint
At the optimum, MRS = wage rate

Willingness to trade leisure for income (MRS) equals ability to trade them (wage)

Optimal work hours are \(h_{0} = T - L_{0}\)
Optimal consumption is \(I_{0} = W_{0}h_{0}\)

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Personal Income Tax





 










The personal income tax affects the budget constraint
Suppose a proportional income tax at rate \(t\) is introduced
The after-tax wage is now \(w(1 - t)\)
Tax causes the budget constraint to pivot inward

Slope is now \(-w(1 - t)\)
Full income is now \(w(1 - t)T\)

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Personal Income Tax

When the budget constraint changes, so does the optimum
Suppose there is a proportional income tax at rate \(t\)
There are two effects of the tax on labour supply







Two Effects of Income Tax on Labour Supply



Substitution effect: leisure is relatively cheaper, so people want more leisure (work less)
Income effect: people are poorer, so they want less leisure (work more)





The effect on labour supply is therefore ambiguous

If substitution effect > income effect, labour supply decreases
If income effect > substitution effect, labour supply increases

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Personal Income Tax





 










Graph shows when substitution effect > income effect

Budget swivels down
Person optimizes at lower indifference curve
Leisure increases from \(L_{0}\) to \(L_{1}\)
Work hours decrease from \(h_{0}\) to \(h_{1}\)

Happens when people are more willing to trade income for leisure

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Personal Income Tax





 










Graph shows when income effect > substitution effect

Budget swivels down
Person optimizes at lower indifference curve
Leisure decreases from \(L_{0}\) to \(L_{2}\)
Work hours increase from \(h_{0}\) to \(h_{2}\)

Happens when people are less willing to trade income for leisure

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Think About It
A single parent working full-time faces a new income tax increase. Would you expect the substitution effect or the income effect to dominate their labour supply decision? How might your answer differ for a secondary earner in a high-income household?

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Personal Income Tax

In reality taxes are not flat

Canada has a progressive income tax system
Higher income is taxed at higher rates

This implies that the budget constraint becomes kinked

As income goes up, the tax rate increases
When the tax rate changes, the slope changes

The basic principles are the same

Substitution and income effects still apply
Labour supply effect is still ambiguous

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Personal Income Tax





 










Graph shows a progressive income tax with three brackets
Tax rates are \(t_{3} > t_{2} > t_{1}\)
Slope changes at each kink

First kink happens with work hours \(h_{0}\)
Second kink happens with work hours \(h_{1}\)

Graph shows increased leisure, but effect is ambiguous

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Evidence on Labour Supply

The theory discusses effect of tax *holding all else equal**
In statistical work, this is not easy to do

Many factors affect labour supply
Isolating the effect of taxes is difficult








Empirical Findings



Elasticity of hours worked for working age men is between -0.2 and 0.2
For women it is between -0.2 and 0.5





Means that a reduction in wage based on income tax has a small effect on work hours
Effect on labour force participation is larger

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Individual vs Group Effects

We simplified the discussion by analyzing one specific type of person
But tax changes affect many types of people differently
A change from a flat to progressive tax might

Increase the tax rate for some people
Decrease the tax rate for others

The way they react will be different and for policy analysis we need to consider the group effects

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Human Capital

Taxes can affect decisions about education and training
We saw that taxes affect an individual’s optimal labour supply at each wage
If a tax increases the optimum hours at each wage, it would increase the desire to get education/training

This would make the worker more productive, and increase their wage
Could lead to further increases in supply

The reverse would happen if tax decreases optimum hours at each wage

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Total Compensation

Wages are not the only part of compensation

There are non-wage benefits like health insurance, retirement contributions, etc.

If taxes rise, firms may switch to non-taxed forms of compensation
The effect of the tax may be muted if firms can do this easily

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Expenditures

Governments use tax revenues to fund public services
That spending may itself affect labour supply

Spending on child care would increase supply
If spent on recreational facilities, parks, etc., may decrease supply

Need to think about this from a general equilibrium lens

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Introduction

As just noted, governments tax labour income to raise revenue
The tax revenue collected from this exercise is the tax rate times the tax base

Tax base is the amount of income earned
Which in our model is \(w \times h\)

So the tax revenue is \(R = t \times w \times h\)
As we saw, if the substitution effect is larger than the income effect, higher tax rates reduce labour supply
Means that as \(t\) increases, \(wh\) decreases

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Laffer Curve






The Laffer Curve


The relationship between tax rates and tax revenue. Tax revenue is zero at both 0% and 100% tax rates. Initially as tax rates rise, revenue rises, but at some point further increases in tax rates reduce revenue.




The fact that higher tax rates may reduce labour supply has implications for tax revenue
Initially as tax rates rise, revenue rises
But at some point, further increases in tax rates reduce revenue

Because the reduction in labour supply is large enough that the tax base shrinks significantly

title: EC313 - Taxation
text: Laffer Curve

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Laffer Curve

The Laffer Curve suggests there is an optimal tax rate when it comes to revenues

At the peak of the curve where additional increases in tax rates do not increase revenue

Also suggests that when tax rates are too high, reducing them could increase revenue
However, determining the optimal tax rate is difficult in practice

Depends on how responsive labour supply is to tax changes
Empirical estimates suggest we are not near the peak of the Laffer Curve for labour income taxes in Canada

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Think About It
Politicians sometimes argue that cutting tax rates will “pay for themselves” through higher economic activity and therefore higher revenue. Under what conditions would this claim be true, and why do most economists believe Canada is not currently in that situation?

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Introduction

In addition to labour supply, taxes affect saving
Saving is important because it funds investment

Investment leads to capital accumulation
Capital accumulation leads to economic growth

Taxes affect saving through reductions in the return

Interest earned through saving counts as income
That income is taxable

In this section we will look at how taxes affect saving behaviour in a life-cycle model

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Life-Cycle Model

The life-cycle model assumes individuals plan their consumption and saving over their lifetime
To keep things simple, we consider two time periods

Present and future

Individuals have preferences for consumption in both periods

Represented by indifference curves

They also have a budget constraint based on their income in both periods

Says that the present value of consumption equals the present value of income

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Life-Cycle Model

Algebraically, the budget constraint is

\[ c_{0} + \frac{c_{1}}{1 + r} = I_{0} + \frac{I_{1}}{1 + r} \]

Where

\(c_{0}\) = consumption in present period
\(c_{1}\) = consumption in future period
\(I_{0}\) = income in present period
\(I_{1}\) = income in future period
\(r\) = real interest rate

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Life-Cycle Model

You can plot this on a graph with \(c_{0}\) on the x-axis and \(c_{1}\) on the y-axis
Rearrange to get \(c_{1}\) on left side

\[ c_{1} = (1 + r)(I_{0} - c_{0}) + I_{1} \]

Slope of budget constraint is \(-(1 + r)\)

Consuming a dollar today means giving up \((1 + r)\) dollars tomorrow

When a person consumes \(I_{0}\) today, they consume \(I_{1}\) tomorrow

The budget line passes through \((I_{0}, I_{1})\)

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Life-Cycle Model





 










Graph shows intertemporal budget constraint
Slope is \(-(1 + r)\)
Optimal consumption occurs where budget constraint is tangent to indifference curve
In this case, the person saves in period 0 to consume more in period 1

Saving is the difference between income and consumption in period 0

title: EC313 - Taxation
section: Tax on Interest Income with Deductible Interest
text:
Tax on Interest Income with Deductible Interest

Now suppose there is a tax on interest income at rate \(t\)
A person who saves $1 in period 0 receives interest \(r - rt\) in period 1

Because the interest earned is taxed they must pay \(rt\) on the interest
This lowers the return

Means that foregoing $1 in period 0 leads to consuming \(1 + r - rt = 1+(1-t)r\) in period 1

The after-tax interest rate is \(r(1 - t)\)

title: EC313 - Taxation
section: Tax on Interest Income with Deductible Interest
text:
Tax on Interest Income with Deductible Interest

A person who borrows $1 in period 0 will need to pay interest \(r - rt\) in period 1

They pay interest \(r\)
But because it is tax deductible they save \(rt\) on taxes
Means that total interest paid is \(r - rt\)

Means that borrowing $1 in period 0 leads to foregoing \(1 + r - rt = 1+(1-t)r\) of consumption in period 1

The after-tax interest rate is \(r(1 - t)\)








Note


Whether saving or borrowing, the after-tax interest rate is the same when interest is deductible.

title: EC313 - Taxation
section: Tax on Interest Income with Deductible Interest
text:
Tax on Interest Income with Deductible Interest





 










Graph shows effect of tax on interest income on optimum
Tax rotates budget constraint around \((I_{0}, I_{1})\)

Slope falls from \(-(1 + r)\) to \(-(1 + r(1 - t))\)
Passes through \((I_{0}, I_{1})\) because no tax paid if no saving/borrowing

Two effects of taxation

Substitution effect: opportunity cost of consumption today is lower, so consume more today (save less)
Income effect: lower real income, so consume less in both periods (save more)

Total effect is ambiguous

title: EC313 - Taxation
section: Tax on Interest Income with Deductible Interest
text:
Tax on Interest Income with Deductible Interest





 










Graph shows case when saving increases

Income effect > substitution effect

Saving increases today
But consumption in both periods falls

title: EC313 - Taxation
section: Tax on Interest Income with Deductible Interest
text:
Tax on Interest Income with Deductible Interest





 










Graph shows case when saving decreases

Substitution effect > income effect

Saving falls today
Consumption increases today, but falls in the future

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Think About It
Young workers early in their careers tend to earn less and may need to borrow, while older workers closer to retirement tend to save. How might removing the tax deductibility of interest payments affect these two groups differently, and what are the implications for intergenerational fairness?

title: EC313 - Taxation
section: Tax on Interest Income with Nondeductible Interest
text:
Tax on Interest Income with Nondeductible Interest

The deductibility of interest payments is important

It made the cost of borrowing the same as the return to saving

Without deductibility, the after-tax interest rate for savers and borrowers differs

A saver who saves $1 in period 0 receives interest \(r - rt\) in period 1
A borrower who borrows $1 in period 0 must pay interest \(r\) in period 1

This creates a kink in the budget constraint at the point where consumption in both periods equals income

title: EC313 - Taxation
section: Tax on Interest Income with Nondeductible Interest
text:
Tax on Interest Income with Nondeductible Interest





 










Graph shows the budget constraint without deductible interest
When the person saves (\(c_{0} < I_{0}\)), the slope is \(-(1 + r(1 - t))\)
When they borrow (\(c_{0} > I_{0}\)), it is \(-(1 + r)\)
The budget constraint is kinked at \((I_{0}, I_{1})\)

Pivots downward to the left of that point
Stays the same to the right

title: EC313 - Taxation
section: Tax on Interest Income with Nondeductible Interest
text:
Tax on Interest Income with Nondeductible Interest

For savers prior to the tax, the effects are the same as with deductible interest

Substitution effect: consume more today (save less)
Income effect: consume less in both periods (save more)

For borrowers prior to the tax, there is no effect

The after-tax interest rate is unchanged at \(r\)
No substitution or income effect

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Additional Considerations

Models are intentionally simplifications of reality to help us understand key mechanisms
The analysis is based on real interest rates, but most saving is done with nominal rates

Inflation and indexation can affect the real return after tax

There is more than one interest rate in the economy

Different types of saving have different tax treatments and returns

Life cycle model may not be a very good representation of how people behave

Some people are not able to borrow the optimal level
Others are not good at saving

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Evidence on Saving

Researchers have analyzed the effect of taxation on saving







Key Finding


The interest elasticity of saving (responsiveness of saving to interest rate changes) is around 0.5, and varies by demographics including age.




Results show that the response to taxation is small
Generally a hard econometric analysis

Many factors affect saving behaviour
Isolating the effect of taxes is difficult

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Savings Vehicles in Canada

Canada has several ways to save




Registered Pension Plans (RPPs)

Tax deductible contributions, taxed withdrawals

Registered Retirement Savings Plans (RRSPs)

Tax deductible contributions, taxed withdrawals




Tax-Free Savings Accounts (TFSAs)

Non-deductible contributions, tax-free withdrawals

Other specialty ones like RESP, FHSA, etc.

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Savings Vehicles in Canada

One way to encourage saving is to increase limits on these vehicles
Not clear that this would encourage new saving

People may just shift existing saving into these vehicles
Existence of other savings methods means people can substitute

Empirical work gives mixed results

Tax deferred savings plans increased savings in the 1970s
More recently, increasing RRSP limit had little effect on total saving

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Capital Taxation

Taxing capital lowers the real return to investment
As such, it may reduce the incentive to invest, and therefore capital accumulation and productivity
Some argue that we should not tax capital income for this reason







Debate on Capital Taxation



Empirical studies show saving not that responsive to returns
In an open economy, domestic saving is used to fund domestic investment, but it may instead flow abroad
For economic efficiency, should tax factors that create the least excess burden

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Housing and Saving

When we think of capital, it is usually machines

Used to produce goods in manufacturing

Housing is also part of capital

Used to produce housing services
Generates income for some households








Preferential Tax Treatment of Housing in Canada



No tax on imputed rent for owner-occupied housing
No capital gains tax on primary residences





Leads to distortions in saving behaviour by encouraging investment in housing over other assets

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Housing and Saving

To see the effect, consider a household choosing between housing and other assets



Investing \(K\) in a stock:

Earn \(R'\) dollars in money income
Also earn \(C'\) in capital gains
These are taxed, so overall return is \(\frac{(1-t)(R' + C')}{K}\)


Investing \(K\) in housing:

Earn \(R\) dollars in imputed rent (an in-kind return)
Also earn \(C\) in capital gains
These are not taxed, so overall return is \(\frac{R + C}{K}\)



Tax treatment favours housing

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Housing and Saving

What would the pre-tax return on the stock have to be to equalize after-tax returns?

Set after-tax returns equal:


\[ \frac{(1-t)(R' + C')}{K} = \frac{R + C}{K} \]

Rearranging gives:

\[ \frac{\frac{(R' + C')}{K}} {\frac{R + C}{K}} = \frac{1}{(1-t)}\]

Pre-tax stock return has to be \(\frac{1}{(1-t)}\) times the housing return to be equally attractive

If \(t = 0.25\), stock return has to be \(\frac{1}{0.75} = 1.33\) times housing return

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Housing and Saving

Estimated foregone government revenue from non-taxation of capital gains on housing is around $10 billion per year
No estimates from non-taxation of imputed rent, but it would be higher
Preferential tax treatment distorts saving behaviour

Encourages investment in housing over other assets
Funds may not flow to their most productive uses

There are also some policies that affect rental prices of housing, which distort behaviour

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Discussion
Canada’s preferential tax treatment of housing has been in place for decades, and housing now represents a large share of household wealth. If the government were to remove the capital gains exemption on primary residences, who would benefit and who would be harmed? What political and economic obstacles make reforming housing taxation so difficult?

title: EC313 - Taxation
section: Changes in Tax Treatment of Housing
text:
Changes in Tax Treatment of Housing


Should we tax imputed rent?

Would increase government revenue
But would be difficult to administer
Could reduce homeownership rates
Politically not feasible


Principal residence exemption

An ongoing debate
Since 2016 Canadians must declare a principal residence and its purchase price
Also report the disposition (sale)

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Introduction

People invest in different types of assets

Stocks, bonds, mutual funds, real estate, etc.

These assets have different returns and risk profiles
May also have different tax treatment
By changing the real return, taxes will alter the portfolio composition

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Portfolio Composition

Imagine a simplified world with two assets

Cash: safe, but no return
Bond: positive return on average, but some risk of loss

Prior to taxes, an investor decides on how much to hold of each
Suppose then the government levies a tax on bond returns

Collects taxes if there is a positive return
Allows losses to be deducted from other income

Two effects

Average return: because the tax reduces what the investor keeps, it reduces the return
Risk: because losses can be deducted, it reduces the risk of holding the bond

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Portfolio Composition

Lower return makes the bond less attractive
Lower risk makes the bond more attractive
Overall the effect is ambiguous

Without loss deduction, likely it would be less attractive to hold bonds

Thus taxes affect portfolio composition, but effect can be complicated

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Summary

Income taxation affects labour supply through substitution and income effects
The Laffer Curve shows the relationship between tax rates and tax revenues
Taxes on interest income affect saving behaviour through substitution and income effects
Preferential tax treatment of housing distorts saving behaviour towards housing
Taxes affect portfolio composition by changing the return and risk of different assets

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
References

Rosen, Harvey S., and Lindsay M. Tedds, and Trevor Tombe, and Jean-Francois Wen, and Tracy Snoddon. Public Finance in Canada. 6th Canadian edition. McGraw-Hill Ryerson, 2023.
Gruber, Jonathan. Public Finance and Public Policy. 7th edition. Worth Publishers, 2022.

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
iClicker Question
The compensated price elasticity of demand is \(-0.25\) for gasoline and \(-1.0\) for restaurant meals. As in our model, supply of both is horizontal and the two goods are unrelated in consumption. To raise a given amount of revenue with the least excess burden, the tax rate on gasoline should be:
A) One-quarter of the rate on restaurant meals
B) The same as the rate on restaurant meals
C) High enough to raise all the revenue, with no tax on restaurant meals
D) Four times the rate on restaurant meals
E) Whatever rate makes the two taxes raise the same revenue

Answer: D. The inverse elasticity rule gives \(t_G / t_M = \eta_M / \eta_G = 1.0 / 0.25 = 4\). A is the most common slip: the ratio flipped. B is neutral taxation, which minimizes excess burden only if leisure could be taxed too, or if the elasticities happened to be equal. C overshoots: the rule equalizes the percent drop in quantity across goods, so both goods carry some tax. Loading everything onto gasoline pushes its marginal excess burden per dollar above the meal tax’s. E aims for equal revenue, but the condition is equal marginal excess burden per extra dollar of revenue, not equal revenue.

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
iClicker Question
Ski-lift tickets and work boots have the same price elasticity of demand. Leisure cannot be taxed. Which tax structure raises a given revenue with less excess burden, and why?
A) The same rate on both, because their elasticities are equal
B) A higher rate on lift tickets, because skiing is a complement to leisure
C) A higher rate on work boots, because they are a substitute for leisure
D) A higher rate on lift tickets, because skiing is a luxury and this makes the tax more progressive
E) No tax on lift tickets, because pushing people from leisure toward work adds to the distortion

Answer: B. Taxing goods but not leisure makes leisure relatively cheap. Taxing a complement to leisure makes leisure less attractive, which works like the leisure tax we cannot levy. A is the inverse elasticity rule on its own; it ignores how each good relates to leisure, which is what Corlett-Hague adds. C reverses the rule: goods that go with work should get the lower rate, since taxing them discourages work. D picks the right policy for the wrong reason: Corlett-Hague is an efficiency argument, not an equity one. E treats any change in behaviour as a distortion. Here the untaxed leisure is the distortion, and nudging people back toward work offsets it.

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
iClicker Question
A provincial ferry is a natural monopoly: average cost falls as trips increase, so marginal cost is below average cost. Assume no regular rider would stop riding because of a fixed annual fee. Which pricing scheme gives the efficient number of trips with no excess burden anywhere, including in whatever pays for the ferry’s costs?
A) Charge marginal cost per trip
B) Charge average cost per trip
C) Charge the price where marginal revenue equals marginal cost
D) Charge marginal cost per trip and cover the deficit from provincial income tax
E) Charge marginal cost per trip, plus a fixed annual fee for each rider

Answer: E, the two-part tariff. The per-trip price equals marginal cost, so riders take the efficient number of trips. The fixed fee covers the deficit, and because nobody quits over it, it works like a lump-sum tax on riders: it changes no decision at the margin. A gets the quantity right but leaves a deficit that has to be paid somehow. D pays it, but the income tax distorts labour supply, so the excess burden has moved rather than gone, and non-riders pay for a service they don’t use. B breaks even, but price is above marginal cost, so some trips worth more than they cost aren’t taken. C is the unregulated monopolist: profits and the largest deadweight loss. The assumption in the question matters: in practice a fixed fee can drive off occasional riders, which is the two-part tariff’s weak spot.

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
iClicker Question
Ann earns $90,000 and Bo earns $30,000. They have identical utility functions with diminishing marginal utility of income, and the government needs $20,000 in revenue. The government can pay transfers as well as collect taxes. Under Edgeworth’s model, the tax system that maximizes social welfare has:
A) Ann paying $40,000 and Bo receiving $20,000
B) Each paying $10,000
C) Ann paying $15,000 and Bo paying $5,000
D) Ann paying all $20,000 and Bo paying nothing
E) Ann paying $30,000 and Bo receiving $30,000

Answer: A. With identical utility and diminishing marginal utility, moving a dollar from the richer person to the poorer one raises total utility, right up until after-tax incomes are equal. Total after-tax income is $120,000 - $20,000 = $100,000, so each ends with $50,000: Ann pays $40,000 and Bo receives $20,000. D is the trap: Edgeworth does not just tax the rich, it transfers to the poor as well. E equalizes incomes but forgets the government’s revenue. B is an equal lump-sum tax; C is a proportional tax at one-sixth of income. Bridge to the next slide: in a large population, full equality means almost every extra dollar anyone earns is shared out, a marginal rate near 100%. If people work less under that rate, the fixed-income assumption fails.

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
iClicker Question
Chris and Dana have the same income and are equally well off. Chris spends spare money on craft beer; Dana spends spare money on concerts. The province puts a new tax on beer only. Under the utility definition of horizontal equity, the beer tax is:
A) Equitable, because the tax does not depend on income
B) Equitable, because Chris could switch to concerts and avoid the tax
C) Equitable, because both face the same tax rate on beer
D) Impossible to judge, because utility cannot be observed
E) Not equitable, because Chris ends up worse off than Dana

Answer: E. The utility definition asks whether people who were equally well off before a tax are equally well off after it. Chris either pays the tax or changes plans to avoid it; Dana is untouched. B is the trap: switching to concerts avoids the tax but still leaves Chris worse off, because Chris preferred beer, and that loss is what the definition counts. C is equal treatment on paper: everyone faces the same rate on beer. The utility definition judges outcomes, not rules, so that doesn’t settle it. It doesn’t pass the rule definition either: taxing one taste and not another is the kind of distinction that test questions, like the book’s angel-food-versus-chocolate-cake example. D confuses a practical objection with the verdict: in practice we can’t see utility, but here we are told they start equally well off. A treats horizontal equity as a test only for income taxes, but it applies to any tax.

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
iClicker Question
Which of these is tax evasion rather than tax avoidance?
A) Splitting pension income with a lower-income spouse
B) Moving from Ontario to Alberta for its lower provincial income tax
C) Deducting a home office for a room that is really a guest room
D) Holding savings in a TFSA so the investment income is not taxed
E) Selling a stock in January instead of December to report the gain in a lower-income year

Answer: C. Evasion is illegal: not paying tax you legally owe, here by claiming a deduction you aren’t entitled to. Avoidance is legal: changing what you do so that you legally owe less. A and B are the traps. Both are done mainly to cut taxes and can feel like dodging, but the tax rules allow pension-income splitting, and where you live sets which province’s tax applies. Wanting to pay less tax is not what separates the two; misreporting is. D and E are ordinary avoidance: using a shelter the law provides, and timing a sale.

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
iClicker Question
In the evasion model, the benefit of each dollar of income hidden is the tax rate \(t\), and the marginal cost of evading rises with the amount hidden. The tax rate is cut from 30% to 25%, and nothing else changes. What happens to evasion, and why?
A) It falls, because a lower tax rate raises the marginal cost of evading
B) It rises, because a lower tax rate lowers the marginal cost of evading
C) No change, because the chance of getting caught and the penalty are the same
D) It falls, because each dollar hidden now saves less tax
E) It falls, because people have more after-tax income and need to evade less

Answer: D. The marginal benefit line drops from 0.30 to 0.25 per dollar hidden. The marginal cost curve doesn’t move, so the two now cross at a smaller amount evaded. A and B put the tax rate in the wrong curve: in this model \(t\) is the benefit of evading, and the cost depends on the chance of an audit, the penalty and attitudes to risk. C assumes only enforcement matters. E tells an income-effect story the model doesn’t have. If someone asks: when the penalty is a multiple of the tax evaded rather than the income hidden, the expected penalty moves with \(t\) too. For someone who cares only about expected income the two effects cancel, so the rate cut changes nothing; with risk aversion the cut can even raise evasion (Yitzhaki 1974, not in the text).

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
iClicker Question
A province offers a tax amnesty: anyone who reports unpaid tax from past years pays what they owe with no penalty. The government promises it will never offer another one. How could the time inconsistency problem make evasion rise afterward?
A) It can’t, because the amnesty only covers taxes from past years
B) It can’t, because the government has promised in public and taxpayers will take it at its word
C) Another amnesty will tempt the government later, so people expect one and evade now
D) The amnesty lowers the penalty for evading this year
E) Honest taxpayers see evaders let off and become less willing to comply

Answer: C. Before anyone evades, the best policy is a firm “never again”. Once evasion has happened it is in the past, and forgiving penalties to collect the back taxes is attractive, so the promise is not credible. Taxpayers who expect another amnesty see a lower expected cost of evading today. A is static thinking: the amnesty applies to the past, but expectations about the next one shape behaviour now. B assumes the government can commit, which is exactly what time inconsistency says it can’t. D misreads the policy. E is a real worry (tax morale), but it is a different mechanism: it doesn’t depend on the government’s incentive to break its promise.

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Politics and Optimal Tax

Imagine a government wants to tax society to raise revenue
People consume three goods: \(X\), \(Y\), and leisure \(L\)
Labour supply is fixed, so income is fixed and nobody can substitute into or out of leisure
The government currently taxes only \(X\); its constitution forbids taxing \(Y\)

Inefficient: it raises the price of \(X\) relative to \(Y\), so people switch from \(X\) to \(Y\)

A tax economist suggests lowering the tax on \(X\) and taxing both \(X\) and \(Y\) at the same rate, raising the same revenue

Efficient: the price of \(X\) relative to \(Y\) doesn’t change, so nobody switches
With income fixed, a tax on all spending works like a lump-sum tax: no excess burden
Different elasticities for \(X\) and \(Y\) don’t change this: with leisure fixed, the Ramsey rule itself gives equal rates



Why equal rates, when the inverse elasticity rule said rates should differ? The elasticities in the Ramsey rule are compensated ones: they measure substitution, not the drop in demand from being poorer. Under equal rates nothing people can substitute between changes price: \(X\) relative to \(Y\) is unchanged and leisure is fixed. So there is no substitution and no excess burden, however different the elasticities, and no tax does better than zero. \(X\) and \(Y\) may still fall by different amounts, but that is an income effect, which a lump-sum tax causes too. The inverse elasticity rule assumed goods unrelated in consumption, with all substitution going to leisure. With leisure fixed, the only substitute for \(X\) is \(Y\), so that assumption fails. The general Ramsey rule still works: with income fixed, the compensated own-price elasticity of \(X\) equals minus its cross-price elasticity with \(Y\), so the percent change in compensated demand is \(\varepsilon_X(t_X - t_Y)\) for \(X\) and \(\varepsilon_Y(t_Y - t_X)\) for \(Y\). Setting them equal gives \(t_X = t_Y\), whatever \(\varepsilon_X\) and \(\varepsilon_Y\) are. This is the lump-sum case from the start of the section, where all goods and leisure are taxed at one rate.

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Politics and Optimal Tax

Citizens are cynical

They think the government will implement the tax on \(Y\) but not lower it on \(X\)
View the government as trying to maximize revenue at their expense
In certain situations they might be right

If they are correct, the ban on taxing \(Y\) protects them from an inefficiently large public sector

What looks inefficient to optimal tax theory may be efficient in a larger setting



Some supporting evidence: governments whose tax systems carry large excess burdens tend to grow more slowly (Becker and Mulligan, 2003). The same argument comes up over taxing online purchases: taxing store sales but not online sales distorts where people shop, but opponents say the extra revenue would just feed a public sector that is already too big.

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Rule Definition of Horizontal Equity

The utility definition judges the outcomes of taxation; another approach judges the rules

Rule definition of horizontal equity: taxes should not be capricious or based on irrelevant characteristics
Rules out, e.g., a special tax on red-haired people, even if it were efficient or redistributive

Comparing the three definitions

Traditional: equal income, spending or wealth; but these reflect people’s choices
Utility: equal well-being; but unobservable and biased towards the status quo
Rule: fair rules; but which characteristics are relevant is disputed

Basic idea is that while horizontal equity is desirable, it is hard to define and implement in practice


Which characteristics count? Almost everyone agrees race and religion should not affect tax owed. Marital status is still argued over. Serious disability should count, but how impaired, and how much relief? The definition is vague, but equal treatment of equals stays a powerful idea in tax debates.

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Compliance Costs

Taxpayers also bear compliance costs: their time plus spending on tax help

Personal income tax, 2012: at least $190 per taxpayer, $235 including appeals and planning
GST: 17% of tax collected for firms with sales up to $100,000, 2.65% above $1 million

Administration plus compliance, all taxes: 1.5–1.8% of GDP (Vaillancourt, Roy-César and Barros, 2013)
Some changes have led to smaller costs

Online filing, automatic download of tax forms, SimpleFile for low-income filers
Proposed: the CRA files for lower-income people who owe no tax, from the 2026 tax year



The 2012 figures are from Speer, Palacios, Lugo and Vaillancourt (2014): about five hours on your own return plus two on appeals and planning, or about $108 if you pay someone. Across 26.9 million taxpaying units that is about $6.3 billion, 2.9% of personal income tax collected. Employers’ compliance costs come on top. The 1.5–1.8% of GDP works out to roughly $754–$917 per Canadian. The GST’s administrative cost was also high, about 3% of revenue, well above similar taxes elsewhere.
SimpleFile (by phone, online or paper) has been offered to eligible people with low or fixed incomes since 2018. Automatic filing was proposed in Budget 2025 and is in Bill C-31, the Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 2, which was still in committee in the House of Commons in October 2026. If it passes, the CRA plans pre-filled returns from spring 2027 for the 2026 tax year, reaching up to 5.5 million people by the 2028 tax year. It would not file for anyone who owes tax. Check the bill’s status before lecture.

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Tax Evasion in Canada

Common ways to commit tax fraud

Two sets of books: one real, one shown to the tax authorities
Moonlighting for cash: no record, so the income goes unreported
Bartering: payment in kind is taxable, but seldom reported
Dealing in cash: hard for the CRA to trace

Underreporting is most common among the self-employed: 12–21% of self-employment income goes unreported (Schuetze, 2002)
Size of the underground economy in Canada

Evasion on legal activity: at most 5.2% of GDP; 8–16% of GDP including illegal activity (Pigeon, 2004)



The CRA doesn’t publish its own estimates of tax cheating, so these numbers are rough. The underground economy covers legal work kept hidden from the tax authorities, like cash home repairs, as well as activity that is illegal in itself. The 5.2% figure is Statistics Canada’s upper bound for the legal part.

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Horizontal Equity and Existing Taxes

With identical tastes and free choice, an existing tax system creates no horizontal inequity

People choose knowing the taxes, and wages and prices adjust, e.g. lower pay in jobs with untaxed perks

Inequities come from changes in tax law

People make hard-to-reverse commitments under the old law, e.g. a bigger house because housing is tax-favoured
MacEachen’s 1981 budget: base broadening was attacked for turning incentives people relied on into “loopholes”

Hence the saying: “the only good tax is an old tax”
Transitional equity: how to change tax regimes fairly, e.g. by phasing reforms in
The utility definition depends on the utility ordering before any new tax (i.e. biased towards status quo)


Tax changes can still improve efficiency or vertical equity, so “don’t change anything” doesn’t follow. One way to ease the transition is to announce a reform now and start it a few years later. Finding fair ways to change tax regimes is hard, and there isn’t much research on it. The status quo point: the utility definition treats the pre-tax ordering as if it had special ethical standing, and it is not obvious why it should. For assets such as housing, the adjustment is capitalization, as with the land tax in the incidence section: the tax advantage gets built into the price, so whoever owns the asset when the law changes takes the gain or loss.

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Choosing the Optimal Tax

Government picks \(t\) and \(\alpha\) to maximize social welfare
It must raise a set amount of revenue, so a bigger grant needs a higher \(t\)

Picking \(t\) fixes \(\alpha\): the problem comes down to choosing one tax rate

A higher \(t\) pays for a bigger grant: more redistribution
But it also discourages work: more excess burden
The optimal \(t\) balances the two


Each person pays \(tY - \alpha\), so tax is linear in income. Revenue is not linear in \(t\): as \(t\) rises people work less, average income falls, and each extra point of tax raises less than the last. That shrinking base is the cost of a higher \(t\); without it nothing stops the rate at 100%, which is Edgeworth’s answer. If asked where the grant comes from: average tax collected is \(t\bar{Y} - \alpha\), so a revenue requirement of \(R\) per person gives \(\alpha = t\bar{Y} - R\). After-tax income is then \((1-t)Y + t\bar{Y} - R\), a weighted average of your own income and the average, with \(t\) the weight on the average. Because excess burden rises with \(t^2\), the first bit of redistribution is nearly free, so the optimal \(t\) is above zero; the rising excess burden keeps it below 100%.

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Personal Income Tax Revenues


All governments, 2022: about 36% of tax revenue, not all revenue as in the table (OECD average 24%), and about 12% of GDP
Federal government, 2024–25: $234.3B, 45.9% of federal revenue and 7.6% of GDP


Table 17.1 covers all levels of government and runs to 2019. The two current lines use different measures, so keep them apart: the OECD figure is a share of total tax revenue for all governments in 2022 (Canada 6th highest of 38 countries), from OECD Revenue Statistics 2024. The federal figure is a share of all federal revenue in 2024–25, from the Fiscal Reference Tables 2025.
The book’s Table 17.2 compares personal income tax as a share of GDP in 2020: Canada 12.5%, the US 10.5%, the UK 9.5%, Australia 11.6% and Sweden 12.4%. Canada looks more like the countries with big welfare states than like those without.

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Administration and Filing

The Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) collects income tax for Ottawa and every province except Quebec

Provinces accept the federal definition of income; Quebec residents file two returns

Until 2000, provinces levied “tax on tax”: a percentage of federal tax owed
By 2001 all had moved to “tax on income”: each applies its own rates and credits to federal taxable income
The system relies on self-assessment: if you owe tax, you file by April 30

The self-employed file by June 15, but any balance is still due April 30

Many people who owe nothing file anyway to collect the CCB, the CWB and the Canada Groceries and Essentials Benefit (formerly the GST/HST credit)

Even so, about 12% of working-age adults did not file (Robson and Schwartz, 2020)



Under the tax collection agreements the CRA collects provincial tax at no charge, as long as the province accepts the federal definition of income. Provinces can set their own credits, but the further those get from the federal ones, the more the CRA charges to run them. Quebec has run its own income tax since 1954. Example of tax on tax: federal tax of $5,000 and a provincial rate of 50% meant $2,500 of provincial tax.
The late-filing penalty only applies if you owe tax. The non-filer figure is from Robson and Schwartz (2020), using 2012 tax data: about 10–12% of Canadians, 12% of working-age adults. Non-filers miss out on benefits they are entitled to. Automatic filing for low-income people who owe no tax is still only a proposal (Bill C-31); it is not law.

title: EC313 - Taxation
section: Steps 1–3: From Total Income to Taxable Income
text:
Steps 1–3: From Total Income to Taxable Income










Step 1 adds up income from taxable sources (line 15000). Step 2 subtracts the first group of deductions, mostly pension contributions and costs of earning income, to get net income (line 23600). Net income is what most income-tested benefits use. Step 3 subtracts a second group, such as losses carried over and the northern residents deduction, to get taxable income (line 26000).

title: EC313 - Taxation
section: Steps 4–6: From Taxable Income to Tax Payable
text:
Steps 4–6: From Taxable Income to Tax Payable








Step 4 applies the rate schedule to taxable income. Step 5 subtracts the nonrefundable credits, most of them 14% of a set amount in 2026. Provincial tax repeats steps 4 and 5 with the province’s own rates and credits. Refundable credits come after all this: they are paid out even if no tax is owed.

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Practical and Conceptual Problems

Business expenses: only income net of costs adds to the power to consume, but the line is hard to draw

A home-office desk that is also good furniture; a business lunch that is also a nice meal (50% of meal costs are deductible)

Capital gains: hard to measure until the asset is sold

Easy for traded shares; hard for art, wine, collectibles, crypto and NFTs

Imputed rent: homes and other durables yield services nobody pays for

Every house is different; cars and boats yield services too

Household production: valuable, but there’s no market price

Cooking, child care, home repairs, yard work

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Evaluating Haig-Simons


Fairness

Horizontal equity needs every source of income in the base

Otherwise people with equal incomes pay different tax

But equal income need not mean equal well-being

Same income from pleasant brain work or unpleasant physical work



Efficiency

Taxing all income alike is neutral

Untaxed imputed rent pulls too much investment into housing

But neutral is not least distorting

Inelastic sources like land rent can be taxed more with no excess burden (Chapter 16)









Bottom Line


H-S is a benchmark, not a rule: judge each departure on its merits




Brains versus brawn: two people with the same income, one in pleasant office work and one in hard physical work in poor conditions. The first is better off, so is it fair to tax them the same? Land: the supply of unimproved land is perfectly inelastic, so a high tax on land rent causes no excess burden. McLure’s point is that optimal tax rules ignore how hard they are to administer and need a lot of information, so we shouldn’t throw H-S away either. The Carter Commission’s recommendations were built on H-S, and the 1971, 1981 and 1987 reforms drew on them.

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Departures from Haig-Simons

Canada’s base is a hybrid of an income tax and a consumption tax

The Carter Commission (1966) and the 1971, 1981 and 1987 reforms moved it toward H-S

Some income is left out, or taxed only later

Left out: imputed rent, employer-paid health and dental plans, gifts and inheritances
Taxed later: employer pension contributions, when the pension is paid

Capital gains get special treatment

Only half of a gain is taxed, and only when the asset is sold (realized)
Capital losses can only offset capital gains

Exemptions remain

Gains on a principal residence are not taxed
Lifetime exemption on farm, fishing and small-business shares: $1,275,000 in 2026



Capital gains history: exempt before 1971; half taxed from the 1971 reform; a $500,000 lifetime exemption in 1985, cut to $100,000 in 1987 and ended for real estate in 1992 and for other assets in 1994. The share taxed went to two-thirds in 1988 and three-quarters in 1990, then back to half by 2000. The 2024 plan to raise it to two-thirds was cancelled, so 50% stands. Losses beyond gains can be carried back three years or forward indefinitely. The lifetime exemption was raised to $1.25 million in June 2024 and is indexed.

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Deferral, Lock-In and Deemed Realization

Taxing gains only at sale defers the tax

The deferred tax is an interest-free loan from the government, so the asset grows at the pre-tax return
E.g., the $5 of tax not paid in year 1 earns $1 in year 2 ($0.75 after tax)
Hence the accountants’ line that taxes deferred are taxes saved








Lock-In Effect


Because selling triggers the tax, owners hold on to assets they would otherwise sell, so capital doesn’t flow to its best use




At death, gains are deemed realized: taxed as if the assets were sold

Unusual internationally; property left to a spouse rolls over tax-deferred



The example from the last two slides: under accrual the owner pays $5 at the end of year 1; under realization that $5 is owed but stays invested, and earns 20% ($1) in year 2. Half of the $1 is taxable at 50% when the asset is sold, so the owner keeps $0.75. Check: after year 2 the realization asset is worth $144 with $11 of tax owed on the $44 gain, so $133.00 net, against $132.25 under accrual. The unpaid tax keeps growing ($5, $11, $18.20, $26.84, then $37.21 paid at sale), and the earnings on it build the gap to $10.50 by year 5.
Many tax shelters are just ways of deferring tax. US studies of realization-based capital gains taxes do find a lock-in effect. Deemed realization means half the gains accrued over a lifetime are taxed in the year of death, so whatever the heirs inherit has already been taxed. That is one reason Canada has no inheritance tax.

title: EC313 - Taxation
section: Should Capital Gains Be Taxed Lightly?
text:
Should Capital Gains Be Taxed Lightly?

Optimal tax theory supports a preference no more than H-S does
Arguments for a preference, and the doubts about each

Gains are windfalls, or reward waiting: but work involves sacrifice too
It spurs investment and risk-taking: not clearly, and there are cheaper ways to do it (Chapter 18)
It offsets inflation: true, but a lower rate is a crude way to adjust for it
Much of it is corporate income: the overall rate depends on corporate tax too (Chapter 21)

Verdict: measured against H-S, Canada’s treatment of capital gains is mixed


Mixed: there has been real movement toward H-S since 1971, but only half of realized gains is taxed, accrued gains go untaxed, and the principal residence, farm and small-business exemptions remain. On sacrifice: one could just as well argue that labour income deserves a preference because work is unpleasant, while capital gains only require waiting. There is no convincing way to rank which income takes more sacrifice.

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Employer Benefits, Gifts and Inheritances

Employer contributions to registered pension plans are not taxed until the pension is paid

Nor is the investment income the fund earns along the way
H-S counts both as income when they accrue, but taxing them is seen as politically infeasible
Employer-paid health and dental plans are also left out

Gifts and inheritances are not taxed as income

Most industrialized countries tax them separately, through estate or gift taxes (the US among them)
Canada and Australia are the exceptions (Chapter 20)



Contributions are limited, but within the limits the pension plan is a tax deferral: no tax until money comes out, often at a lower rate in retirement. For gifts and inheritances, the fact that the donor paid tax on the money doesn’t matter under H-S, any more than a shopkeeper’s income is exempt because customers paid with after-tax dollars. Deemed realization at death partly fills the gap left by having no inheritance tax.

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Deductions Change Prices

Suppose spending on good \(Z\) is deductible and your marginal tax rate is \(t\)

Each $1 spent on \(Z\) cuts taxable income by $1 and saves \(t\) in tax

Example: \(Z\) costs $10 and \(t\) = 40%: each unit saves $4 in tax, so it really costs $6







Effective Price with a Deduction


A deduction lowers the price of \(Z\) from \(P_Z\) to \((1-t)P_Z\)




Two consequences

The relative price changes, so the quantity of \(Z\) bought changes too
The higher your marginal rate, the more a deduction is worth to you

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Main Deductions

Child care: up to $8,000 per child under 7, $5,000 aged 7–16, $11,000 with a disability

Claimed by the lower-earning parent, up to two-thirds of their earned income

Union and professional dues, and employment expenses the employer doesn’t repay
Moving expenses when the move is to earn income
Carrying charges: interest on money borrowed to invest
Spousal support: deducted by the payer, taxed to the recipient

The payer is treated as passing the recipient’s income along
Child support under orders made after April 1997 is neither deducted nor taxed



All of these are costs of earning income, so deducting them gets closer to taxing net income: without child care, many parents couldn’t take paid work. The taxpayer has to be able to show the CRA the money was spent, and each deduction has rules to stop unreasonable claims. The child care limits are not indexed.

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Interest Deductibility and Tax Arbitrage

Interest on consumer loans and on the mortgage on your own home is not deductible

Consumer interest is just the price of buying something sooner
Imputed rent isn’t taxed, so the interest that finances the house isn’t deducted

Interest on money borrowed to earn taxable income is deductible







Tax Arbitrage


Borrowing with deductible interest to invest in an asset whose return is untaxed or tax-preferred




Example: \(t\) = 40%, borrow at 10% (6% after tax), invest tax-free at 7.5%
Mostly helps high-income people, and is hard to police


In the example, keep borrowing as long as the gap lasts: every dollar costs 6 cents a year after tax and earns 7.5 cents. Limits in practice: there are only so many tax-free investments, and nobody can borrow without limit. The CRA watches for it; for example, interest on money borrowed to put into an RRSP is not deductible. But money is fungible, so it’s hard to prove what a loan was for. High-income people gain most because they face higher rates and borrow more easily, and a lot of effort goes into finding schemes and policing them.

Home Buyers’ Plan: borrow up to $60,000 from your RRSP for a first home, repaid over 15 years
All are departures from H-S; whether they raise total saving is unclear


RRSPs and RPPs defer tax: it pays most if your rate is high while you contribute and low when you withdraw. The TFSA (2009) is the reverse: no deduction going in, nothing taxed coming out, and nothing in it counts toward income-tested benefits such as OAS and the GIS. The government expected about half the TFSA benefit to go to seniors. RESP earnings and grants are taxed in the student’s hands, usually at a low rate. The FHSA (2023) is deductible going in and untaxed coming out if used for a first home. On saving: people may just move savings they already had into the plans, so the evidence on whether total saving rises is unclear.

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Tax Credits Change Prices Too






Refundable vs Nonrefundable Credits


A refundable credit is paid out even if it exceeds the tax owed; a nonrefundable credit can only reduce tax to zero




A credit at rate \(x\) lowers the price of \(Z\) from \(P_Z\) to \((1-x)P_Z\), the same for everyone
A deduction’s value depends on your tax rate; a credit’s does not

A $100 credit is worth $100 to anyone who owes tax
A $200 deduction is worth $100 at a 50% rate, $60 at 30%

Most federal credits are set at the lowest rate: 14% in 2026

So a credit is worth the same as a deduction only for someone in the lowest bracket



Example of a percentage credit: with a 50% credit for research spending, $1,000 of R&D costs the taxpayer $500. The 14% rate follows the cut to the lowest federal rate (15% until mid-2025). A temporary top-up credit for 2025–2030 keeps 15% on credit amounts above $58,523, so people with large claims don’t lose from the rate cut.

Age amount: $9,208 for 2026, reduced at higher incomes. Medical: the credit covers costs above the lesser of 3% of net income or $2,890; in effect the tax system insures large medical costs, with a deductible. The boutique list also includes the volunteer firefighter credit. Enhanced CPP contributions (since 2019) and CPP2 (since 2024) are deducted rather than credited. Unused tuition amounts can be carried forward or transferred. The CWB, 2026, single person: 27% of working income above $3,000, up to $1,665, then reduced by 15% of adjusted net income above $27,392, gone at about $38,492; a disability supplement adds up to $860. The Canada Groceries and Essentials Benefit replaced the name GST/HST credit in July 2026 and is 25% higher for five years. The CCB (2016) replaced several child benefits and is clawed back as family income rises. Boutique credits come and go: the children’s fitness credit ended after 2016 and the digital news subscription credit after 2024. Each costs little, which makes them a cheap way to be seen supporting something.

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Charitable Giving: Credit vs Deduction








Canada: Credit (Ontario, 2026)


For gifts above $200 in a year:

Federal credit of 29% (33% on income in the top bracket) plus Ontario’s 11.16%
Each $1 given costs about $0.60 ($0.56 in the top bracket): much the same for every donor











United States: Deduction (Stylized)


A gift is deducted from taxable income:

The price of $1 given is \(1 - t\)
$0.76 in the 24% bracket, $0.63 in the 37% bracket
Richer donors pay a lower price






Canadian estimates put the price elasticity of giving above 1

Giving rises by more than the price falls, so charities gain more than the government loses



On the first $200, the Ontario credits are 14% federal plus 5.05% provincial, so a $100 gift costs $80.95. Above $200: 29% + 11.16% = 40.16%, a price of about $0.60, or about $0.56 for a donor with income in the top federal bracket. Donations qualify up to 75% of net income, and unused donations carry forward five years.
The US side is stylized. From 2026, US itemizers deduct gifts only above 0.5% of income, and people who don’t itemize can deduct up to $1,000.
If the price elasticity is zero, the credit is just a bonus for people who would give anyway. With a 40% price cut and an elasticity above 1, giving rises by more than 40%. Whether the government should subsidize gifts to private charities at all is a separate debate.

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Credits or Deductions?

Before 1988, Canada used exemptions (deductions) for the taxpayer, spouse, dependants and age

A $5,000 exemption saved $2,500 at a 50% rate but $1,000 at 20%

The 1987 reform turned them into credits, worth the same dollar amount to everyone
But the choice is not that simple

Rates can be adjusted to offset any loss of progressivity
If the aim is to measure ability to pay, e.g., unavoidable medical costs, a deduction fits
If the aim is to change behaviour, it depends on who responds: a subsidy to someone who won’t change is wasted



A credit cuts the price by the same percentage for everyone; a deduction cuts it by more for people in higher brackets. If people’s responses differ, it can make sense to offer them different prices, so credits are not obviously more efficient. They are simpler and widely seen as fairer.

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Tax Expenditures: For and Against


Criticisms

Estimates assume people wouldn’t change behaviour if a break were removed
They need a benchmark tax base, and there is no agreed one

One person’s loophole is another’s fair adjustment

They imply that untaxed income belongs to the government


Defences

Tax breaks are subsidies, so review them regularly like spending
They let us compare spending through the tax system with direct spending on the same goal
They allow benefit-cost analysis of tax breaks



The third criticism is philosophical: calling a tax break “spending” assumes the money was the government’s to begin with, when in a democracy property is private unless the public decides to transfer it. Defenders say the concept carries no such ideology. It is just a way of recognizing that the tax system is one of the main ways government subsidizes things, and rough estimates are still useful.

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Rates and Brackets

Canada has a progressive rate structure: higher incomes pay a larger share in tax
It uses brackets: ranges of taxable income, each with its own rate







Marginal vs Average Tax Rates



The marginal tax rate is the tax on an additional dollar of income: what matters for decisions to work, save and invest
The average tax rate is total tax divided by total income





The rate in a bracket applies only to the dollars that fall in it
Federal rates ran from 4% to 29% in 1917 and 15% to 84% by 1949; there are 5 federal brackets today


In 1917: a 4% normal tax on income over $1,500 (singles) or $3,000 (others), plus a supertax of 2% to 25%, for a top rate of 29% over eight brackets. War pushed rates to 15–84% by 1949. Since then rates have been compressed. Brackets: 15 by 1949, 10 after the 1981 reforms, 3 after 1987, later 4 and now 5. Simplicity was one of the five goals of the 1987 reform, but the Income Tax Act is still long enough to be called the accountants’ and lawyers’ full employment act.

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Factors Affecting Marginal Rates

The statutory rate is the one in the law; what you keep from an extra dollar can be very different







Effective Marginal Tax Rate


The share of an extra dollar of earnings lost to income tax, payroll taxes and reduced benefits




Surtaxes: Ontario is now the only province with one
Payroll taxes: CPP 5.95% and EI 1.63% of earnings, up to annual maximums
Clawbacks: benefits shrink as income rises, which works like a tax

CCB, Canada Groceries and Essentials Benefit, EI benefits, OAS
CWB, single person, 2026: 27% phase-in above $3,000 (up to $1,665), clawed back at 15% from $27,392 until gone at about $38,492



2026 payroll details: CPP is 5.95% of earnings up to $74,600, plus 4% (CPP2) up to $85,000; EI is 1.63% of insurable earnings up to $68,900. Employers pay matching amounts. Clawbacks: the CCB is reduced as adjusted family net income rises, at rates that depend on the number of children; OAS is clawed back at 15% of income above a threshold; regular EI benefits are clawed back at 30% for higher-income claimants. Each of these adds to the marginal rate over its income range. The CWB phase-in is a negative tax: each extra dollar earned brings 27 cents more benefit. A disability supplement adds up to $860.

Marginal Tax Rates: A B.C. Example

Over 50% in parts of the $30,000–$57,000 range, as the CWB, CCB and GST credit clawbacks stack on tax and payroll taxes
The rate does not rise smoothly with income



From the book’s Table 17.6 (Milligan’s Canadian Tax and Credit Simulator), which counts federal and provincial tax, the employee’s CPP and EI, and the CWB, CCB and GST credit clawbacks. The book’s last row is wrong: at $210,371 the federal rate rises from 29% to 33%, so the combined rate is 49.80%, not 40.00%. The chart uses the corrected value. The book’s table also ends the CCB clawback at $76,137, which looks too early for two children, so treat the right half of the chart as illustrative. 2019 CWB parameters were lower than today’s.

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
Effective Versus Statutory Rates

Statutory rates can mislead about who really pays, for three reasons

Preferences: taxable income can be much smaller than a comprehensive measure of income
Incidence: taxes can be shifted, so the person who pays isn’t necessarily the person who bears the tax (Chapter 14)
Excess burden and compliance costs: taxes cost more than the revenue they raise (Chapter 15)

So statutory rates say little about how progressive the system really is

Lower rates on a broader base could be just as progressive, with less excess burden and less evasion



A tax-free benefit doesn’t let you escape the tax entirely. Say your marginal rate is 50% and your employer spends $500 on dental coverage that you value at $300. As wages, the $500 would leave you $250. You take the coverage, but you’d have preferred the cash, so the tax system still leaves you worse off. Similarly, when an investment is tax-favoured, its pre-tax return tends to fall by the value of the break, an implicit tax, so effective rates on high-income investors are higher than their tax bills suggest.

title: EC313 - Taxation
text:
The Flat Tax






Flat Tax


One rate applied to everyone and to every kind of income, with no deductions except a personal exemption and strictly defined business expenses




For given revenue, the key trade-off is between the exemption and the rate

A bigger exemption makes average rates more progressive, but needs a higher rate
One rate of 25% (Alberta) to 30% (Quebec), with a $7,231 exemption, would have matched 2000 revenue (Emes and Clemens, 2001)










For



Less excess burden and less incentive to cheat
Simpler, so lower administration and compliance costs
Can stay progressive through the exemption











Against



May shift the burden from the rich to the middle class
Hard to confirm, since it depends on who really bears the tax






Canada moved partway: the top federal rate fell from 43% (1981) to 29% (1988) as the base broadened; a 33% top bracket was added in 2016


The 1981 and 1987 reforms are the moves toward a flat tax: the top federal rate went from 43% to 34% in 1982 and 29% in 1988, and the base was broadened by dropping deductions and taxing more interest, dividends, capital gains and fringe benefits. Alberta had a single 10% rate from 2001 until the NDP government added brackets in 2015–16. Recent reforms show a clear preference for progressive rates.

title: EC313 - Taxation
section: Three Principles for the Tax Unit
text:
Three Principles for the Tax Unit

Canada taxes the individual, and always has

Some countries tax the family: income is pooled and taxed on one return

Three principles most people find appealing







Three Principles



The income tax should have increasing marginal tax rates
Families with equal incomes should pay equal taxes
Two people’s taxes should not change when they marry or move in together: the tax should be marriage neutral





With increasing marginal rates, no system can satisfy both 2 and 3


Principles 2 and 3 have broad support, though both are argued over. Support for increasing marginal rates is weaker, but they seem to have wide political support. Principle 2 holds other things equal, including family size.

The Marriage Penalty
